news.title: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. What's their next move?
news.text:
CASA GRANDE, Ariz. (AP) — Chris Martinez feels like Donald Trump has made a fool of him.

The 28-year-old maintenance technician from Casa Grande, Arizona, voted for the Republican president expecting to get a thriving economy and no wars.

Instead, gas prices are so high that Martinez returned one of his vehicles to the lender, he shifted his food shopping to a discount grocer and he has watched as the United States has spent months in conflict with Iran.

“He’s doing nothing for us, to benefit us," Martinez said, adding, "I got duped and I feel like a dummy.”

As a group, Latinos shifted toward Trump two years ago, helping return him to the White House with a Republican-controlled Congress. Now, many like Martinez are souring on the president and his party.

The path to a U.S. House majority runs through heavily Latino districts in states such as Arizona, Colorado and Texas, where Democrats are counting on disaffected Trump supporters to swing back their way. It is unclear whether Democrats have sealed the deal with voters who lack strong allegiance to either party.

An Arizona farming town faces a transition

Casa Grande, the town of 70,000, sits at a crossroads between Phoenix and Tucson. There is a quaint downtown surrounded by master-planned developments offering affordable housing for people priced out of larger cities. Gated golf-course communities attract retirees.

Much of the town is at the northern tip of Arizona’s 6th Congressional District. Republican Juan Ciscomani is seeking a third term. Two years ago, Ciscomani won by 2.5 percentage points and Trump won by less than 1 point. 

This time, Ciscomani is subtly creating distance from Trump. The congressman talks up his immigrant story — he was born in Mexico and moved to the U.S. as a kid — and frames himself as independent and bipartisan. 

Ciscomani's Democratic opponent is JoAnna Mendoza. The former Marine emphasizes her own hardscrabble upbringing as the daughter of immigrant farmworkers who worked the fields close to Casa Grande. 

“People trust you if they know that you came from the community and understand their way of life,” Mendoza said in an interview earlier this year. 

Most Hispanic voters disapprove of Trump

Trump made broad gains among Hispanics during the 2024 campaign.

Now, about 6 in 10 Hispanic voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the presidency, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll from October. More than 7 in 10 disapprove of his performance on the economy.

Their potential shift away from Republicans this year would be driven by anti-Trump sentiment, not a love of Democrats, said Mike Madrid, a political consultant who wrote “The Latino Century,” a book about Latino voters, and co-hosts “The Latino Vote” podcast. 

Latinos are in the midst of a “dealignment,” rejecting strong associations with both parties because neither is speaking effectively to working class economic concerns, he said. 

Hispanics are about evenly split on their view of the Democratic Party, according to the October AP-NORC poll. Their views of the Republican Party are more negative, with 55% having an unfavorable view and 38% having a favorable one.

The economy is at the center of a Colorado contest

On a recent morning in Denver, Democratic state lawmaker Manny Rutinel stood before a crowd of union carpenters and rolled up his sleeve to show off a scar from when he sold his blood more than 100 times to make ends meet.

“I’m the son of a single mom. She came to America to give me the American Dream. We worked hard for this country,” Rutinel said.

Rutinel is challenging Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, which stretches from blue-collar Denver suburbs to energy-rich farm and ranchland in the northern part of the state. Latinos are the district’s single largest ethnic group, and both the incumbent and challenger are Hispanic. Evans won by less than 1 percentage point while Trump won by 2 points.

Rutinel has focused relentlessly on the economy. Evans, a 40-year-old former police lieutenant, has portrayed Rutinel as having a record as a left-wing activist and liberal lawmaker.

Jose Montalvo, a 47-year-old trucker, voted for Evans even though he supported Democrat Kamala Harris for president in 2024. He likes to split his ticket between the parties but does not think he will do that this year. Montalvo is frustrated by Trump's handling of gas prices, saying “I blame him for the fuel side of things." That is a criticism he extends to all Republicans.

Maria del Carmen Rojas, a naturalized citizen who has lived in the United States for 36 years, said she is shocked that any Latinos could back Trump and a Republican Party that she thinks regularly denigrates immigrants. 

“We Latinos contribute very much to this country, the taxes we pay, the service we provide,” she said. 

Frustration mounts in Texas' Rio Grande Valley

A wooden sign that said “need prayer?” sat on a table with free Bibles along a busy suburban walking trail in Edinburg, Texas, on a hot October evening. The town is part of the state's 15th Congressional District, which Trump carried by 18 points but is now viewed as a top Election Day battleground.Standing behind the table, Thomas Centrella, 42, said he has grown disillusioned with politics. He doubts he would ever vote for a Democrat but said he might skip elections or turn independent in the future. Maria Elsa Gonzalez, who is retired, said she will again support the district's Republican congresswoman, Monica de la Cruz, instead of Democrat Bobby Pulido, a Tejano music star. Speaking in Spanish, Gonzalez said Pulido “doesn’t have any preparation other than a pretty face and the fame of singing pretty.”Priscilla Olivarez, 46, a public education teacher, is undecided in the midterms. She grew up as a Democrat and voted Republican in the last presidential election. Today, she is disappointed with an economy where costs seem to be growing faster than wages and she often digs into her own pocket to help pay for things in the classroom.“I stand independent right now because I don’t agree with either side right now,” she said.___Riccardi reported from Denver and Gonzalez from Edinburg, Texas.

news.title: Meet the Democrats breaking through in the country’s most pro-Trump town: ‘Tough nut’
news.text:
Political outreach can be an uphill battle. But for Democrats trying to make inroads in Roberts County, Texas, it can feel more like a full-bore sprint into a brick wall.

This rural patch of the Texas Panhandle has long been described as America’s most pro-Trump county with more than 94 percent of its voters backing Donald Trump in each of the past three presidential elections.

By contrast, the county’s Kamala Harris voters could all fit comfortably on a school bus. This year’s Democratic primary voters could share an Uber.

“We just haven't been able to get any traction there,” Sean Birkenfeld, president of Panhandle Democrats, a regional political action committee, told The Independent.

In interviews, Democrats described the Sisyphean task of gaining a foothold in Roberts County where Fox News plays in local businesses, Trump signs dot lawns and the party of Franklin Roosevelt has spent decades in hibernation. Some suspect there are actually more Democrats than election returns suggest but that they remain “closeted,” reluctant to advertise their politics for fear of backlash.

Roberts County, located about 80 miles northwest of Amarillo, is home to roughly 870 people. Its economy revolves around agribusiness and oil, and it is one of just three Texas counties that still prohibits alcohol sales. Its only city is Miami, pronounced “My-am-uh.”

The county earned its reputation as Trump’s most loyal in 2016, when he won 94.58 percent of its votes — the highest Republican vote share of any county in that election. Its support has remained remarkably consistent: Trump took 96.18 percent of the vote in 2020 and 95.63 percent in 2024.

For some residents, Trump represented a promise that people like them would not be overlooked. “I feel like Trump has my back, I hope he doesn't prove me wrong,” local resident John Faith told a news outlet in 2016. 

Another resident, Steve Porter, emphasized strength, immigration and jobs in an interview with ABC News in 2018. “I realized that we needed a president who believed America was great. Greater than all other countries,” he said.

Democrats hoping to establish a presence in the county have had their work cut out for them. This year’s Democratic primary drew just three voters, while the GOP’s drew 306.

Mark Nair, the Democratic nominee for Texas’ 13th congressional district, which encompasses the county, said he has visited Roberts County several times. Drawing a crowd has proved difficult.

“Seriously, it's like two people that would come,” he told The Independent.

Birkenfeld’s attempt to organize an event in Roberts County, meanwhile, never reached the point of counting attendees. He contacted people about setting something up, he said, but the plans fell through. “I haven't actually been able to get any engagement,” the political organizer said.

There is currently no Democratic county chair to help make the introductions or rally potential volunteers. The position is vacant, Birkenfeld said, leaving the party without local leadership.

For Nair, the difficulty is not a lack of warmth from the people he meets.

“They're very, very nice people who believe in their community and their family. They really do,” Nair said. “But when it turns to politics, it's almost like you're trying to crack this tough nut.”

He added: “And I can make arguments all day long, but it's difficult because they're kind of stuck into this way of thinking that Trump might do something great for them. It's confusing to me because I don't see the evidence of that.”

For now, some of the work of building a Democratic presence is considerably less ambitious than changing anyone’s mind. 

The Roberts County Texas Democrats Facebook group is administered by Bonny Krahn, who lives hundreds of miles away in rural Hays County. She created county-specific groups across Texas to provide a starting point where Democratic organizations were absent or struggling, with the intention of handing them over as local chairs emerged.

Posts in the group cover the essentials. “This is your next election. Date, time, and place. This is who's on your ballot,” she said, describing the information she shares.

The Roberts County group currently has 19 members.

Organizers suspect the election returns do not tell the whole story of Democratic life in the rural Panhandle. Some supporters, Birkenfeld says, would rather keep their politics to themselves.

“There's not really a better terminology, but they're in the closet,” he said.

A tale, from a few years back, illustrates what publicly breaking with the majority in Miami, the county seat, can mean.

In a 2020 interview with The Mirror, museum curator Susan Bowers said she had grown up in a Republican household but changed her allegiance after studying in Amarillo and training in social work. Her opposition to Trump, she said, had cost her.

“I feel like the black sheep of Miami,” she told the newspaper. “It’s a lost cause trying to convince people Trump should not be in power. Passions here runs so deep. The sad thing is I have lost friends over this.”

The concern about making one’s politics public is familiar to Birkenfeld, who says people across the wider region have reported stolen or defaced yard signs and hostile reactions to Democratic shirts and bumper stickers.

Birkenfeld, said he has experienced hostility in the region first-hand. At an arts event in Potter County, a stranger spotted his shirt emblazoned with the name of a Democratic candidate and approached him.

“Oh, so you're one of those libtards,” he recalled them saying.

But political isolation cuts both ways. Trump supporters in liberal bastions such as New York City have also described feeling stigmatized and keeping their views to themselves.

Despite the difficulty of getting people to turn out Nair believes some residents in Roberts County are questioning what their loyalty to Trump has delivered.

The concerns he hears from people center largely on farming and water rights — the county sits above the largest freshwater aquifer in North America. But he acknowledges the limits of those conversations.

“Now, I know it's not everyone in the county speaking, because when I show up, like I said, most of the people won't come to an event,” Nair said. “But the people that do, they really are very upset that they voted several times for Trump, and they're feeling that… betrayal is a good word.”

Krahn said she’s seen movement in the business of rebuilding local Democratic organizations. She estimated that Texas had about 64 counties without Democratic chairs when she began her work; now, she said, there are about 46.

“So we're slowly going the right direction,” she said.

Beyond the Panhandle, Democrats see an opening to loosen the Republican Party’s iron grip on Texas. The most closely-watched opportunity is the U.S. Senate race, where Democratic state Representative James Talarico is challenging Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton for the seat held by outgoing GOP Senator John Cornyn. 

Recent polling suggests a competitive contest. A UMass Lowell/YouGov survey, released October 8, put Talarico and Paxton at 45 percent each, with 7 percent of voters undecided. A separate Fox News poll recently gave Talarico a narrow advantage, 51 percent to 49 percent, within its margin of error.

In Roberts County, though, the work described by organizers is less about an election night transformation than building something that can last beyond November: finding a county chair, reaching people reluctant to speak up and getting a few more residents to turn out. 

In a place where this year’s Democratic primary drew three voters, even modest gains would mark a start.
news.summary: Democratic voters in the country’s most MAGA county could all fit together in an Uber — but with Trump’s popularity slipping, organizers aren’t giving up, Brendan Rascius learns

news.title: Are You Wearing A MAGA-Coded Outfit? Here's How To Tell.
news.text:
When people think about MAGA aesthetics, beauty often comes up first ― from the oft-criticized “conservative girl makeup” to the so-called “Mar-a-Lago Face” trend in cosmetic surgery. But style watchers say politics can also show up clearly in clothing.

“When I look at fashion today, clothes become a kind of visual language,” Edith Chan, a celebrity stylist and image consultant, told HuffPost. “It communicates values, identity and sometimes politics without a single word being spoken.”

On one end of the spectrum are overt markers like MAGA hats, campaign T-shirts and slogan-heavy merch. Loud garments drenched in red, white and blue also carry a strong association with conservative politics in the modern age.

“But what I find more interesting are the subtle signals, the ones that aren’t political on their own, but start to feel coded in certain contexts,” Chan said. 

Below, fashion historians, stylists and cultural critics break down the pieces, brands and aesthetics most commonly associated with MAGA-coded style for women ― and why they’ve taken on this meaning today.

Of course, none of these signals are hard-and-fast rules. People across the political spectrum wear the same brands, garments and materials. But in today’s hyper-polarized environment, fashion choices increasingly read as cultural shorthand, whether the wearers intend that or not.

Tweed jackets, dresses and Chanel‑adjacent silhouettes seem to have become staples of MAGA‑coded style ― perhaps fittingly so, given Coco Chanel’s complicated political history.

“MAGA got super into searching ‘old money style’ during 2020 and never evolved past it ― mind you, people with old money are not Googling ‘old money style,’” said political commentator and social media personality Suzanne Lambert. “Their sustained hyperfixation seems to be the tweed dress with the buttons on each side, usually with a high collar that cuts off at the neck and makes it look too wide. I think those tweed dresses are becoming the equivalent of a MAGA hat.”

The irony, she noted, is that many of the icons behind this look ― including First Lady Jackie Kennedy ― were Democrats and part of a coastal elite establishment that MAGA politics publicly rails against. And many of today’s versions rely on mass-market or fast-fashion reproductions, a sort of “Shein Chanel,” if you will. 

“There are these really tragic Amazon dupes that are mostly polyester,” Lambert said. “But so many of these Republican staffers working on the Hill very much want to emulate that aesthetic. They don’t even really understand what they are trying to emulate. They just know that it seems aspirational.”

At higher levels of conservative politics, that tweed often comes with a heftier price tag, as seen in former Attorney General Pam Bondi’s jackets or the Oscar de la Renta pieces favored by Fox News personalities. On the fictional side, the wealthy conservative “Gilmore Girls” matriarch Emily Gilmore sported many expensive tweed jackets. 

“It’s this classic look that we associate with conservatism today, very feminine and clean,” said public historian Einav Rabinovitch-Fox. “It’s signaling that these women are maintaining more traditional gender roles, like the Chanel suit is this very traditional, conservative, even sort of old look.”

Former first lady Nancy Reagan wore her fair share of tweed jackets and skirt suits, projecting a look that balanced softness with authority ― polished, feminine and firmly within traditional expectations of womanhood. That visual language continues to shape how conservative women in power dress today.

“It’s a feminine iteration of the traditionally masculine garment ― the suit,” said Maureen Lehto Brewster, an assistant professor of fashion merchandising at the University of Maryland Eastern Shore. “Women in politics have always had to straddle a double bind of gender and double bind of fashion. Do you wear a suit? If so, what kind of suit do you wear? A skirt suit?”

Rather than adopting overtly masculine tailoring, Lehto Brewster said many mainstream Republican women now opt for what critics have dubbed the “Republican Barbie” aesthetic.

“It’s almost like a Fox News anchor look ― throwing out the suit entirely and dressing in this overtly feminine way to reassert patriarchal dominance,” she said. 

That emphasis on masculine dominance is consistent with Trump administration policies and positions. Lehto Brewster also believes the old money aesthetic plays into the MAGA movement’s racial politics. 

“It’s all very class coded,” she said. “A lot of these young women express wanting to look ‘classy,’ but that’s also a very racially coded thing ― who gets to claim that, and who doesn’t.”

One of the most popular tweed dresses among D.C. conservatives is the $298 “Jackie” shift dress from Tuckernuck, a clothing and lifestyle retailer selling a preppy aesthetic that the founders describe as “classic,” “timeless” and “all American.”

Despite leadership that appears politically liberal, the brand has become a staple among conservative women, from Fox News anchors to prominent figures in the Trump administration. The Daily Beast dubbed Tuckernuck “The Brand Dressing MAGA’s Leading Ladies ― Whether It Likes It or Not.”

“I think Tuckernuck has entered the cultural conversation around MAGA fashion less because of overt politics and more because of what it visually represents,” said Chan. “The brand positions itself as ‘your one-stop shop for a fun, full life,’ and that life is clearly framed through an East Coast, upper-middle-class lens ― classic, heritage-inspired, preppy and aspirational.”

Even the brand name is a nod to East Coast elitism: Tuckernuck is a privately owned island near Nantucket, the affluent New England destination where the founders summered as children.

Although that coastal elitism might seem at odds with MAGA’s populist rhetoric, conservative figures appear drawn to the brand’s aesthetic of privilege, stability, femininity and reliability over trend or novelty.

“Tuckernuck doesn’t promote MAGA ideology directly, but its aesthetic aligns closely with values often associated with modern conservatism ― tradition, respectability, family life and understated wealth,” Chan said. “In today’s polarized climate, fashion like this becomes read politically, whether the brand intends it or not.”

Lambert called Tuckernuck a “safe” brand that takes the guesswork out of fashion, and offers an ease and predictability that speaks to the conservative ethos. 

“I love Tuckernuck and actually wear a lot of it ― while also recognizing it’s definitely Republican-coded,” she said. “You might not look like the trendiest girl at the party in Tuckernuck, but the silhouettes and fit are consistent and modest, which is helpful particularly in a Hill setting.”

She also pointed to the jarring contrast between the brand’s “demure” image and the actions of some of its most visible wearers. Donning these “corporate feminine” looks are outspoken political figures who use their power and platforms to promote controversial policies that cause harm.

“When you think about Tuckernuck and then you look at what the Trump administration is doing, it’s pretty obvious that Republicans wearing Tuckernuck is more about assimilation and distraction than curating one’s own style,” Lambert said. “There’s something particularly eerie about Kristi Noem wearing a number you might wear to a girl’s boozy brunch while also being someone who shot her own dog and stands by ICE murdering an American citizen.”

Loud Luxury Handbags

While old money style typically favors “quiet luxury,” the MAGA version seems to mix in conspicuous branding. 

For example, Leavitt’s “White House style ... favored a few of the big international luxury brands ― like Louis Vuitton, Gucci and Jimmy Choo,” said style and cultural commentator Chelsea Perry.

Perry joined other critics in noting that this affinity for European luxury designers seems to contradict the Trump administration’s “Made in America” policies and rhetoric.

“They’re also designers that even people that don’t spend five hours a day on Pinterest would clock as expensive. Loud luxury,” Perry added. 

The loud luxury vibe tends to show up in bag choices, particularly the logo-filled Louis Vuitton and Gucci pieces carried by several folks in the MAGA orbit, including chief of staff Susie Wiles and first lady Melania Trump.

“People with old money choose high-quality logo-less clothes and try to blend in as much as possible,” Lambert noted. 

Former congressional staffer Beverly Hart, who analyzes the political cues in fashion on TikTok, has called the Louis Vuitton Neverfull “screaming Republican — Trump Republican.” Other loudly branded choices like the pink Marc Jacobs Tote Bag also go into the Republican category for Hart. And for Christian Dior’s Book Tote, she said “It’s giving, definitely doesn’t vote but goes to events at Mar-a-Lago.”

The fascination with conspicuously branded luxury accessories among the MAGA establishment contrasts sharply with the economic reality many Americans face today. 

“To me, it reads as an attempt at signaling economic prosperity,” Perry said. “A sort of ‘Hey! The economy is fine. America is thriving. Our policy decisions are working. You can trust us.’ This becomes more apparent when you look to the daily beauty habits of the regular, working woman grappling with the cost-of-living crisis.”

Pointed-Toe Nude Heels

Last year, Women.com published an article that branded nude pointed-toe heels as “The Bland Shoe Trend That’s Taking MAGA Women By Storm (& We’re Begging For A Style Upgrade).”

“Like many of the aesthetic choices favored on the far right, the shoe feels stuck in a bygone era. At the very least, it reflects a preference for past over present,” the article states.

Nude pointed-toe heels certainly seem to fall into the category of predictability and traditional femininity that characterizes MAGA fashion. 

“The intention of the conservative look is just being seen as cleaner and more feminine to distinguish themselves from leftists ― kind of to say, ‘We’re not like those crazy lesbians or blue-haired liberal college girls or trans people,’” said Rabinovitch-Fox, who authored “Dressed for Freedom: The Fashionable Politics of American Feminism.”

While liberal politicians like Rosa DeLauro, Jasmine Crockett and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez might make bold styling choices, conformity is the name of the game on the other side of the political aisle. 

“With conservative looks, the message is usually about tradition, stability and being put together,” said stylist Ariana Weisner. “There is a focus on neatness and modesty and nothing too experimental.”

“I love a nude pump, but it very much lends itself to the way they want their fashion to be as mindless as possible,” Lambert said. “There’s no thought or creativity.”

One of Hart’s videos about footwear suggests liberals tend to be drawn to chunkier shoes, though she notes that the classic nude sandal style block heel enjoys bipartisan support. 

“That pointed-toe nude heel is classic and traditional,” Lehto Brewster said. “They don’t wear anything that undermines or undercuts traditional gender roles. By contrast, look at what Kamala Harris wore for her February Vogue cover ― Converse sneakers with a suit.”

Large Cross Necklaces

“There’s a religious aspect to the look,” Rabinovitch‑Fox said, who pointed to one specific accessory in addition to general modesty. “You see these really big cross necklaces, which is kind of a clear marker.”

Of course, Christians of all political leanings have worn cross necklaces, and crosses have also cycled through pop culture, appearing recently on decidedly not-conservative celebrities like Chappell Roan and Sabrina Carpenter.

But the decision to wear rather oversized or expensive versions ― especially when paired with tweed and traditional silhouettes ― gives this accessory a distinctly political resonance in recent years. 

“It’s a type of accessorizing that is aligning yourself with traditional values,” Lehto Brewster said. “There was a ‘conservative girl makeup’ video where someone made fun of Karoline Leavitt by doing her makeup and then putting on this giant cross made out of aluminum foil and this cream tweed jacket.” 

Indeed, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt’s affinity for large cross necklaces has sparked jokes and critiques, with many highlighting the juxtaposition between Christian values around honesty and the Trump administration’s tenuous relationship with the truth. 

Puffy Sleeves And Prairie Dresses

Style watchers say long dresses with puffy sleeves ― sometimes called gigot or leg-of-mutton sleeves ― have become another hallmark of MAGA-coded style, particularly with pastel palettes and soft florals. 

“There’s a strong visual nostalgia at play,” Chan said. “As Carolyn Bessette’s 1990s minimalism resurfaces with pencil skirts, tall boots and headbands, it sits alongside an even more idealized ‘trad wife’ look that borrows from the 1800s or 1950s ― pastel dresses, Southern femininity, and a lifestyle narrative centered on domesticity.”

She pointed to the rising demand for equestrian boots and knee-length skirts, which she sees as signaling “polish, tradition and control rather than rebellion.” Silhouettes are shifting with longer hemlines, buttoned-up shifts and modest proportions. It all mirrors “a broader cultural return to traditionalism,” Chan noted. 

“On social media, especially TikTok, aesthetics like trad wife, clean girl, coquette and old money amplify this look and repackage conservative values as aspirational and nostalgic, particularly for younger audiences,” Chan said. “What this really shows is how fashion has become a quiet but powerful way of expressing social and political alignment often without people even realizing they’re doing it.”

Indeed, the move toward modesty coincides with the rise of tradwife influencers who promote traditional gender roles in a way that might not initially read as political ― but are deeply intertwined with right-wing cultural ideology. 

Usha Vance wore a puff sleeve midi dress from Tuckernuck to meet Pope Leo (though in the color black, per protocol for official meetings with the pontiff). 

“They LOVE a long dress with big puffy sleeves,” Lambert said. “When you look at the puffy sleeves and ditsy little patterns,” it’s very much like what you would dress a little girl in. It’s like those Lilly Pulitzer Mommy and Me dresses. It feels childish.”

This infantilizing element of today’s conservative fashion is echoed in Hart’s video breaking down the political signals in accessories, in which she notes that girlish headbands and “anything with a bow” reads as Republican today. 

But Lambert also sees a coquettishness to the trend of long prairie dresses with puffy sleeves, particularly with the more “milkmaid-style” pieces. 

“They feel very much male gaze-coded,” Lambert said. “There’s nothing wrong with wearing a milkmaid dress, but it feels obvious why conservative women would ― they think it looks good for men.”

In that sense, MAGA-coded fashion isn’t just about looking conservative. It’s about signaling who power is for, who it centers and who it excludes.

news.title: A California town’s beaches are washing away. Can its residents turn the tide?
news.text:
San Clemente is one of southern California’s most picture-perfect beach towns – a capital of American surf culture since the 1950s. In two years, 2028 Olympic surfers will compete at Lower Trestles, a world-class surfing beach.

But the town’s longtime cultural and economic driver, its beaches, are now under threat. As pounding waves driven by late-summer storms in the Pacific devour chunks of the California coastline, some of San Clemente’s beaches are growing narrower, the sand increasingly eaten away.

Beach erosion has become a crisis all along the southern California shoreline this year, with towns from Dana Point and Long Beach to Malibu sustaining dramatic damage. But San Clemente is a particular flash point. It’s the place where the major regional train line, which carries $1bn in freight a year and is the nation’s second-busiest passenger line, runs right along the edge of the Pacific Ocean. Severe waves and high tides during big storms at the beginning of September forced the repeated closure of the tracks.

Experts say California’s current season of extreme weather is just getting started. “We’re in for a run of pretty exceptional erosion events if this Super El Niño develops as it’s expected to,” said Sean Vitousek, an oceanographer with the US Geological Survey (USGS).

As the potentially historic El Niño season overlaps with a massive surge of warm water called a Kelvin wave, residents worry it will leave coastal infrastructure in pieces, beachfront properties leveled and more beaches carved away to crumbling slivers of gravel and bare rock.

Donald Trump has continued to deny climate change as a “hoax”, “con job” or scam”. But in southern California, a historically conservative area, the effect of extreme weather events linked to the climate crisis have suddenly become very, very real.

“We’ve been anticipating rising sea levels 50 years from now,” said Hallie Jones, the mayor pro tem of Laguna Beach, California. “This summer proved that sea level rise is already here.”

‘A game of attrition’

On a hot, clear day, Cameron Cosgrove, a San Clemente beach restoration activist, took me to the state beach on the south side of town, where swimmers and sunbathers ambled over the major rail line’s tracks to perch on a very narrow strip of sand that descends steeply into the deep blue water.

“You can see, when it gets steep like this, then you’re just at a game of attrition,” Cosgrove told me. “It’s just a matter of time before the next big wave event will start moving and start taking some of this.”

Big storms at the beginning of September already saw the erosion of some of this coastline creep up to the train tracks. “Severe waves and high tides overtopped the tracks,” according to a spokesperson for the Orange County Transportation Authority (OCTA). The local commuter rail posted a video of sediment next to the tracks crumbling into the sea as waves slammed the shore.

After nearly a century of reliable service, the coastal rail line has been shut down seven times since 2021 for repairs after landslides and surging tides on stretches of the line in San Clemente and further south down the coast. Over the past five years, the closure times “have totaled more than one year”, an OCTA spokesperson confirmed.

There’s no relief ahead. Once considered a gradual problem, coastal erosion is now being discussed more urgently, as the risk of California’s beaches simply disappearing, said Charles Lester, a former head of the California Coastal Commission who now leads an ocean policy center at the University of California, Santa Barbara. California scientists warned in 2023 that sea level rise sped up by the climate crisis threatens to erase between 25% and 75% of California’s beaches by 2100.

This is posing a massive challenge, particularly for leaders of smaller beachside towns whose appeal is built around their ocean access. Orange county, a collection of suburbs clustered between Los Angeles and San Diego, is famous as the birthplace of the Reagan Revolution. Today, the county is more politically purple than deep Republican red – more voters backed Kamala Harris than Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. Some of its most famous beach towns, such as Newport Beach, remain Republican strongholds, favoring conservatism and as little government regulation as possible. But extreme weather and the growing threat to beaches is putting pressure even on Republican political orthodoxies.

Southern California’s wealthy coastal towns are used to breezier weather and lower temperatures than Los Angeles, or the scorching cities of the Inland Empire. But record-breaking heatwaves are changing that.

“It’s October 5 and it’s 90 degrees in Dana Point. Unless there’s Santa Ana [winds], it’s unheard of,” said John Gabbard, Dana Point’s Republican mayor. “The ocean temperature is high. There’s no wind. And that’s not happening just by happenstance. Nobody’s using the words ‘global warming’, but everybody is recognizing that it’s warmer and it continues to be warmer through the past few seasons than it’s ever been in the past.”

In San Clemente, where a majority of residents voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024, Cosgrove, a retired IT executive, is advocating a radical move: he authored a ballot measure that will go before voters in November, asking local residents to voluntarily impose a 1% sales tax on themselves to fund beach restoration and wildfire prevention efforts. A large portion of that tax revenue would be dedicated to replacing what he estimates is the city’s deficit of 4m to 6m cubic yards of beach sand.

Nobody likes taxes, Cosgrove said, but voters need to face what he believes is the stark reality all along the California coast: if local residents don’t pay to protect public beaches from vanishing, it’s not clear that anyone else will.

Shifting sands

Southern California’s wide, sandy beaches are not exactly a natural resource. Many of them were created or expanded with sand dredged up by major midcentury construction projects.

San Clemente’s beaches, for example, were fortified with an estimated 2m cubic yards of sand removed during the creation of Dana Point’s harbor in the late 1960s, Cosgrove said. “We’ve been living off that ever since,” he said.

Since those midcentury construction projects, further development and infrastructure, especially dams on California’s rivers, has blocked the flows of sediment that would naturally restock the beaches with sand, while competition for the available supply of dredged-up or trucked-in sand has grown more intense. This has made the erosion of California beach sand an ongoing issue for decades – but it’s a problem that is now escalating rapidly.

Much of California’s coastline development was completed during the state’s population boom from the 1940s to 1970s – years that happened to be an unusually “calm climate period” along the Pacific Ocean – “not many big El Niños, not a lot of storm damage”, Griggs, the coastline expert, said. “People built on the cliffs, they built on the bluffs, they built on the dunes.”

Since then, stronger El Niño seasons have returned – and this year threatens to be the worst on record.

Beach town residents such as Jones, the Laguna Beach mayor pro tem, who has lived there for much of her 48 years, are used to seeing sand migrate throughout the year. Beach sand is not a static amenity, but a complex system that can shift onshore and offshore, north and south. Scientists refer to each sand system as a “littoral cell”.

During winter storms, Jones said, Laguna’s beaches typically lose sand, but later storms tend to bring it back, a kind of natural restoration. What’s happening now, though, is “not business as usual”, Jones said.

Vitousek, the USGS oceanographer, said the intensity of this year’s coming tropical storms may disrupt beaches’ natural cycles: “You can get this thrashing, where the beach gets fully eroded on the south end, and then fully eroded on the north end,” he said. While beaches can sometimes recover “in a lot of cases, the damage is done. You’ve lost a beach. The waves are now breaking right on the infrastructure, causing damage.”

A few miles north of San Clemente, in Dana Point, the same ferocious Labor Day waves that paused train traffic through San Clemente ripped through a row of coastal residences, leaving 10 homes red-tagged as uninhabitable.

“The damage that we have seen this year has been extraordinary,” Gabbard, the mayor, said. He estimated there had been $33m in damage to private property, and another $25m in damage to the public beach.

Up and down the coast, lesser beach damage in early September served as a warning of what might be coming in the next months: a beachside parking lot was seriously damaged by waves in Laguna Beach, big sections of sand vanished around Balboa Pier in Newport Beach, and a sinkhole opened in the driveway of Nicholas Cage’s coastal mansion in Malibu.

In October, abnormally high tides flooded a low-lying neighborhood of Newport Beach, with local news outlets sharing footage of someone paddling on a surfboard through the streets. Huge waves damaged more homes in Long Beach. A dramatic crack in a cliffside bluff near Laguna Beach forced the continuing closure of part of the Pacific Coast Highway.

Though San Clemente’s Lower Trestles was not one of the hardest-hit beaches in early September, local news outlets have already begun speculating over whether future Super El Niño damage could cause problems for the beach as a major Olympic venue.

‘People don’t want to retreat’

The most common short-term response to pounding waves that wash away local beaches and threaten beachside homes is to armor the shore with sea walls, revetments or simple piles of rocks. This has been a popular tactic, especially in southern California, where an estimated 38% of the coastline is now armored in some way. Half a century ago, in contrast, only 2.5% of California’s total coastline had armoring.

But armoring, though relatively fast and simple, has a hefty long-term cost. Environmentalists, beach-loving residents and California’s powerful coastal commission all warn that building walls to guard the coastline serves as a death knell to the beaches next to them.

Impermeable barriers block sediment from restocking the beach, while waves pounding on the barriers drag existing sand away, said Gary Griggs, a professor at University of California, Santa Cruz, who has been studying the California coastline for more than 50 years. In time, he said, any beach caught between the armoring and the sea disappears.

For beach restoration activists such as Cosgrove, a fully armored, fully beachless California shoreline is the future dystopia they are trying to avert. From San Clemente’s state beach, Cosgrove showed me what the future shoreline might look like, if coastal communities continue to respond to erosion with short-term crisis management of throwing down rocks and putting up walls. He pointed south towards Cypress Shores, one of San Clemente’s gated oceanfront communities. Beneath the clifftop homes, the waves pounded directly onto a revetment, a rocky barrier shielding the rail line and the foot of the cliffs. “They had a 200–ft beach,” Cosgrove said. “They had volleyball courts. They had barbecues. Now there’s no beach. It’s all armor.”

“If we never did sand replenishment, if we just don’t do anything at all, that revetment is the future of San Clemente,” Cosgrove told me. “From one end to the other. It may take 35 years to get there, but it will be that way.”

Environmentalists and some coastal experts say the only viable long-term strategy for the California shoreline is “managed retreat”. That means moving homes, roads and other infrastructure inland from the eroding coast – a response that requires huge amounts of planning, logistics and consensus building, and is about as popular with coastal homeowners and developers as one might expect.

“Most people don’t want to be managed, and most people don’t want to retreat,” said Griggs, the coastline expert. But, he added, “they’re not going to have a choice at some point”.

The centrist option, the one with the most support from across the political spectrum, is simply replenishing the sand on California’s eroded beaches – what Cosgrove is hoping to fund with his San Clemente ballot measure.

“It is a softer option than putting rock down, and it provides some more of that habitation and recreation space,” said Kelsey Ducklow, a coastal resilience coordinator at the California Coastal Commission.

Beaches are “the best natural buffer we have from waves”, Griggs said. “If the beach is narrowed or gone, the waves attack the cliffs directly.”

The problem is that hauling and dumping tons of sand on existing beaches is extremely costly and planning intensive – and not at all guaranteed to last, coastal experts said. Grigg described it as “a very, very temporary fix”.

“One big storm can remove hundreds of thousands of cubic feet [of sand],” Griggs said. At Torrey Pines beach in San Diego in 2001, he recalled, officials brought in 200,000 cubic yards of sand – equivalent to 20,000 dump truck loads, at a cost of more than $2m for that beach alone. “It stayed there for about eight months, during the spring and summer. Right around Thanksgiving, a storm hit, the waves came up, and [it] was gone overnight.”

What does the future hold?

In San Clemente, Cosgrove argued, the city’s beaches, which run between the protective arms of Dana Point and Cottons Point, are more sheltered, allowing new sand to stay within the system of beaches longer. An infusion of sand from 2024, placed with the help of the army corps of engineers, is still providing some cushion for the town’s beaches, he said. In the months he spent collecting signatures at the farmers’ market and local grocery store to get his sand-replenishment measure on the ballot, he heard widespread support for continuing to restock San Clemente beaches with new sand.

What people want to know, he said, is “Can someone else pay for this? Do we have to pay?” Residents want to know why the federal or state government isn’t funding beach replenishment with the taxes they already pay.

One might think that a state as known for government bureaucracy as California might have a statewide beach commission, or at least a state sand fund, to keep one of the state’s primary economic engines from disappearing. It does not. The California Coastal Commission has regulatory power up and down the shoreline and can provide small planning grants to local jurisdictions, but it does not have the kind of money necessary to fund big sand projects, a spokesperson said.

For that, Lester said, coastal cities usually need to go to the federal government and get a congressional appropriation for sand – a process that can easily take a decade, or even two, between when the state approves a replenishment plan and when federal money actually comes through.

In Dana Point, where a majority of voters also supported Trump in 2024, Gabbard is hoping the president will step in to help with emergency funds to help the coastal town’s continuing storm damage.

“Through back channels, I’ve been trying to get to the president to voice our concerns about, not just the homes themselves, but our beaches writ large, to make sure there are funds available to repair what we need to repair,” he said.

One of the many projects needed, he said, is to create a more natural buffer for future storm damage at Capistrano beach by building a sand berm – a single project estimated to cost $16m.

Even when federal funding is approved, cities are usually expected to provide matching funds for a big beach restoration project, Cosgrove said, which is why he thinks the most reliable option is for local residents to raise the money they need for beach restoration themselves, through a 10-year local sales tax. He said he is cautiously optimistic that San Clemente’s tax-skeptic voters will make an exception in November and vote to support wildfire prevention and the town’s beaches.

While the Orange county transportation administration recently pledged to expedite the placement of 690,000 cubic yards of sand to protect the crucial rail line through San Clemente, the timing of the project remains unclear, in part because the project will require “specialized marine dredging equipment”, and, of the US’s few existing machines, “many are committed to other projects months in advance”, an OCTA spokesperson said in a statement.

The state government is currently examining whether the rail line should simply be moved inland to a new location – a project already estimated to cost more than $5bn. The rail runs dangerously close to the ocean in both San Clemente and Del Mar, a town closer to San Diego.

Even if OCTA’s emergency sand restoration project in San Clemente is completed in a timely way, Cosgrove said, the amount of sand the agency has pledged to provide is far too little to restore all the city’s beaches.

In making his pitch to San Clemente voters, including on his Yes on Measure M website, Cosgrove doesn’t talk about the climate crisis, though he said he does see the role the warming ocean is playing in the extreme weather hitting California’s coast.

“I’m just messaging on stewardship and adding sand to our beaches,” he said. “This is the local issue that we’re facing. We can’t affect global climate change, but we can protect ourselves from it by nourishing our beaches. Having wide beaches is the best protection no matter what comes our way.”

Some residents have a less optimistic attitude about efforts to prevent further coastal damage. In San Clemente, Zhen Wu, a city council member, has opposed Cosgrove’s tax measure, telling the Associated Press: “Fighting mother nature is very expensive.”

On a hot October Friday, Kathy Ruiz, of Laguna Niguel, was sunbathing on a mostly-empty Aliso beach, not far from where construction equipment was repairing the Laguna beach parking lot damaged by early September storm surges.

“As far as people expecting the city to protect their homes, I don’t think that’s reasonable,” she said. “I think maybe they shouldn’t have built so close to the beach.”

Some residents want the government to build up sand berms to protect homes against the coming storms, Ruiz said, but she was skeptical.

“Nature is going to take its course,” Ruiz said. “I think all that stuff is in vain.”
news.summary:
Rapid coastal erosion threatens coastal homes and economies, and as Super El Niño rounds the corner, a town is reckoning with the reality of climate crisis

San Clemente is one of southern California’s most picture-perfect beach towns – a capital of American surf culture since the 1950s. In two years, 2028 Olympic surfers will compete at Lower Trestles, a world-class surfing beach.

But the town’s longtime cultural and economic driver, its beaches, are now under threat. As pounding waves driven by late-summer storms in the Pacific devour chunks of the California coastline, some of San Clemente’s beaches are growing narrower, the sand increasingly eaten away.

news.title: Barabak: Despite a blue tide, this Democratic governor is fighting to survive
news.text: With just over two weeks left until election day, Democrats can barely contain their glee. Control of the House seems about to fall into their eager laps. Senate races in states that are normally cardinal red — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas among them — have grown fiercely competitive. And, for the first time since 2010, a Democrat may soon be sitting in the governor's office in more than half the 50 states. As recently as 2017, just 16 of them had Democratic governors — the lowest number in nearly a century. The party owes a big thank you to President Trump, whose political standing seems to be sinking, like a depth charge, lower by the day. The only question is how much damage he inflicts on fellow Republicans. There are, however, exceptions to every political trend, outliers in every election, a contest that zigs when races just about everywhere else are zagging. Oregon, that crunchy and damp citadel of Left Coast liberalism, hasn't elected a Republican governor since President Reagan was midway through his first term. In 2024, Kamala Harris walloped Donald Trump by more than 14 percentage points, extending a decades-long Democratic presidential winning streak. And yet the state's Democratic governor, Tina Kotek, is on the defensive as she fights for a second term in November, burdened by a dismal approval rating and a sense that things have been pretty lousy in Oregon under her leadership. The state "hasn't thrived in the last decade, and certainly hasn't thrived since COVID, the way other states have," said John Horvick, one of Oregon's leading independent pollsters. Kotek, a former speaker of the state House — and a highly effective lawmaker in that role — made some very concrete promises. "She was going to build 36,000 new homes. She was going to improve our educational outcomes and make improvements to behavioral health in the state," Horvick said. "Voters give her poor marks on all those." Most notably, perhaps, the epidemic of homelessness — which has curdled Portland's hipster image and agitated Oregonians more than just about any issue in recent years — hasn't abated under Kotek, despite a promise to make the problem her top priority. The Democrat still remains the favorite to win reelection. Oregon's gubernatorial races tend to be closer than presidential contests and voters have been shown a reluctance to heave their governor from office, even when they tell pollsters they're not happy with the incumbent or the state of their state. "We watch this movie every four years in Oregon, where it looks really, really close and then, in the end, the Democrat wins," said Kari Chisholm, a political strategist in Portland. That may happen again. But Kotek's travails show the perils of incumbency this angry election season, even for a Democratic swimming with a blue tide. Thirty-six states are electing governors in November. Most of the contests lean toward one party or the other, like in California, where Democrat Xavier Becerra appears a shoo-in to replace Gavin Newsom. But a dozen races are at least somewhat competitive, including toss-ups in Georgia, Nevada, Ohio and Wisconsin. All of the hardest-fought contests are in states that Trump carried in 2024 — several by double-digits — with Oregon being the lone exception. Kotek, who's been rated one of the least popular governors in America, is facing a rematch against Christine Drazan, a former GOP state House leader who now serves in the state Senate. In 2022, she lost narrowly lost to Kotek, 47% to 44%, in a three-way contest. Unlike four years ago, Kotek has a gubernatorial record to defend and the case Drazan makes against her is succinct. “Tina Kotek told Oregonians that she would solve the problems and challenges facing our state,” Drazan said in the candidates' first debate this month. “She hasn’t.” In a recent Fox News interview, Drazan elaborated. "We have record high businesses that have gone out of business, bankruptcies, businesses that are leaving, family bankruptcies are at an all-time high," Drazan said, exaggerating some. “Oregon is uniquely bad right now. It's not a national issue, it's here at home." Suggesting the state's problems are indigenous is an obvious effort to lay responsibility on Kotek and absolve Trump, whose policies — ruinous tariffs, a reckless war, budget cuts — have slashed healthcare benefits, stoked inflation and driven fuel prices to all-time highs. Further distancing herself from the Republican brand, Drazan has undergone a distinct makeover since winning the GOP primary in May. “Tough. Tested. Conservative," is no longer the descriptive shorthand she uses on her campaign website. Now it's “Mom. Public Servant. Champion for All.” Drazan's revised campaign biography also omits her opposition to various Democratic-backed policies, such as gun control, and her culture-warrior vow to "protect girls' sports and keep men out of their locker rooms." Instead, the Oregonian newspaper noted, her emphasis is now affordability and relatability. Despite that, Kotek has continued wielding her sharpest-pronged political weapon, tying Drazan — an "out-of-touch MAGA extremist," in her campaign's parlance — to the unpopular president. "I think we all know that there have been a lot of challenges facing our state and they're still coming at us because of the confusion and disruption coming from Washington, D.C.," Kotek said during the candidates' third and final debate last week. "It's just a fact. It's upending who we are as a state and it is ... making it harder for us to solve the problems that we have ahead of us." Passing the buck and pointing her finger is not exactly a message of triumph, uplift and achievement, but it may be enough to win Kotek a second term. Grudgingly.
news.summary: In Oregon, a progressive bastion, voter discontent has incumbent Tina Kotek on the defensive. Her struggle shows the perils of incumbency this angry election season.
news.author: Mark Z. Barabak

news.title: Shame on me for being fooled by Donald Trump
news.text:
If Trump did do drugs and/or drink, he might use them as an excuse. That would be bad enough. But to do these things in one’s right mind suggests that there is something very wrong with that mind; the phrase ‘second childhood’ occurs, when an aged person behaves in a way we might more readily associate with a badly-socialised brat. At the age of 80, Trump does seem like a particularly silly child, perhaps one who has consumed an excessive amount of E-numbers at his own birthday party and is one gummy sweet away from jumping on the table and announcing that he’s the king of the castle and those funny foreign kids are dirty rascals. 

He has previous, of course, to his grotesque Carnival Of The Animals variations online. This spring he appeared to depict himself as Jesus Christ during a spat with the Pope, and come summer he could be ‘seen’ shooting the breeze with JFK. It’s likely that he is very lonely, having seen off a good number of his IRL friends by allowing his monstrous ego out to play once too often. Regrettably, I know how this feels.

But another aspect of his online life provides the one meagre excuse I have for so enthusiastically cheerleading for the brute. (Apart from his very sound determination to keep cross-dressers out of girls and women’s sport.) Earlier this year, Trump made an AI video of himself as a doctor, diagnosing the highly irritating likes of Whoopi Goldberg and Rosie O’Donnell with ‘Trump Derangement Syndrome’ (TDS). Like Brexit Derangement Syndrome before it, this was indeed a very real phenomenon which saw sufferers robbed of all critical facilities. Amusingly, being affected by it appeared to turn the victim into a copy of the person they hated most, pontificating and fulminating to the point of insensibility. 

The wholesale attempted weaponising of the celebrity class in favour of first Joe Biden and then Kamala Harris (the first senile, the second extremely silly) turned out to be the dampest of squibs. This was not surprising to anyone who has come across the hilarious fact that Hillary Clinton’s 2016 list of celebrity backers warrants a Wikipedia page of its own, so long is it. If anything, the celeb endorsements were vote-winners for Trump, as ordinary people have a stubborn tendency not to listen to the views of people who have spent their working lives doing things they love and being rewarded with kings’ ransoms. 

But of course, TDS is no excuse for my foolhardy fawning over this man. I should have drawn the line at the persistent sex-pest allegations, the ludicrous call for a ‘united Ireland’ and, more than anything, his repeated disrespect towards President Zelensky. This has now come to a head after Trump attempted to humiliate this dignified and stoic man by mocking his clothes. The US President’s cuddling up to Vladimir Putin seems to know no limits now.

I’m ashamed that it took me so long to see sense; I swallowed that ‘the enemy of my enemy is my friend’ cliche to a point where I couldn’t seem to see past it. Like a long relationship you’ve invested a lot in, I’d defended him to my incredulous friends for so long that to back down would make me look like an atrocious judge of character – which I am, and always have been, and so it shouldn’t have come as a surprise. 

I would say in my defence that the years of tolerance – affection, even – of many intelligent people for Trump says a lot about the shocking quality of the Democratic candidates. But I do believe that we are witnessing the end of America; not as an actual country, but as a magic kingdom of the mind, the place of which F. Scott Fitzgerald wrote:

France was a land, England was a people, but America, having about it still that quality of the idea, was harder to utter – it was a willingness of the heart…

Donald J. Trump, ranting in his isolated grandeur, unwilling to offer the assistance that could make or break Ukraine’s war effort, makes a fitting figurehead for this downfall. I’m not conceited enough to believe that my opinion ever swayed anybody – but shame on me for being fooled by him for so long.

news.title: Trump Maintains Defiant Message In Kentucky Midterm Rally, Makes Dubious Claims About Republican Popularity
news.text: President Donald Trump held a midterm campaign rally in support of GOP candidates in Highland Heights, Kentucky on Saturday. In spite of record low approval ratings and polls showing that races for the House and Senate in traditionally Republican-leaning states will be close, the president projected a defiantly optimistic message throughout the event."I started the [campaign] rallies and all of a sudden the Republican party is starting to look very good. We're winning," the president told his supporters. "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot because when I'm on the ballot ... we always won," Trump continued.It is unclear whether this strategy of emphasizing his own supposed personal popularity will work for Trump. As of October 17, 60% of Americans disapprove of Trump, compared to just 37% who approve, a New York Times tracker shows. Polls also now show that the Democrats are currently increasing their chances of winning a majority in the Senate, which was seen as unlikely.Most polls show that victory for the Democrats in the House is all but assured, with Harvard University forecasting that the Democrats have a 91% chance of winning the Lower House.One of the reasons for Democrat optimism is the party's apparent newfound competitiveness in traditionally conservative seats, such as Texas, where Trump beat Democrat presidential candidate Kamala Harris by over 13.5% in the 2024 presidential election.Trump claimed that a poll that came out on Saturday morning showed that Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate in Texas who Trump called the "greatest attorney general in the history of Texas," was ahead in the race against his Democrat challenger James Talarico, who Trump dubbed "Talafreako."It is unclear which poll Trump was referring to; according to RealClearPolling's (RCP) Texas Senate poll tracker, a poll conducted by InsiderAdvantage on Tuesday and Wednesday gave Paxton a one point advantage over Talarico, but the tracker showed that the vast majority of polls conducted by other organizations put Talarico ahead.The current RCP average for polls conducted between September 24 and October 14 gives Talarico a lead of just over two percentage points. A victory for Talarico would mark the first time a Texas Democrat has won election to the Senate in nearly four decades.During his visit to Kentucky, Trump also reiterated many of the claimed triumphs that have become a key feature of his recent campaign rallies: he praised his own administration's imposition of tariffs on Canada, its handling of ongoing hostilities with Iran - he claimed "we beat the s*** out of them" - and the government's decision to rename both the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America.The president also repeatedly attacked the previous Democrat administration of President Joe Biden for allegedly opening the border, presiding over the "worst inflation in American history, [and] the highest energy prices in American history."Under Biden, inflation hit a 40-year, as opposed to an all-time, high of 9.1% in June 2022. However, by the end of his term in January 2025, inflation had fallen to 3.0%, which is lower than the inflation rate recorded in September 2026, which was 3.7%. The national average monthly electricity bill hit its all-time high in mid-2026, under TrumpGas prices indeed reached an all-time high of over $5 per gallon in mid-June 2022 - a phenomenon that was largely attributed to the Russian war with Ukraine - but are currently much higher than the average price across Biden's full term, which was about $3.45 per gallon. As of October 17, daily gas prices are $4.31 a gallon.Despite his apparent confidence about Republican victory, there were some possible indications in Trump's speech of the potential for a Democrat win; the president told voters repeatedly to get out and vote in large numbers, called the election "the most important midterm in the history of our country" and warned the Kentucky crowd that if Democrats win, "they're going to open your borders."
news.summary: The president held a rally on Saturday in which he touted the supposed successes of his two terms in office, attacked his domestic opponents and claimed that the Republican party is gaining ground in the polls.
news.author: Raphael McMahon

news.title: Trump traveling to Kentucky to rally supporters ahead of midterms
news.text:
President Trump is heading to Kentucky Saturday to rally supporters and shore up Republicans facing unexpectedly competitive races — including a House contest that could put another seat at risk for the GOP.

Trump’s trip to Highland Heights, in Northern Kentucky, also puts him just across the Ohio River from battleground Ohio, where former US Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is trying to reclaim his seat from US Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who was appointed to fill the vacancy left by Vice President JD Vance.

Trump has visited Ohio four times during his current term, including two trips this month. During one visit, he joked about examining Husted’s backside — a reminder of the state’s importance as Republicans fight to preserve their 53-47 Senate majority and narrow 218-214 House majority.

The race is considered a pure tossup, in a state Trump carried against former Vice President Kamala Harris 55-44 in 2024, according to the Cook Political Report.

Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said Trump’s decision to campaign in a state he won handily was a troubling sign for Republicans.

“I don’t take any vote for granted” he told reporters this week. “But the fact that in the weeks leading up to this midterm election, the president’s coming to a state he won by 31 points that he believes he needs, suggest to me that Republicans are in big trouble,” he said, slightly padding Trump’s 30-point 2016 victory.

Trump’s rally also gives him access to Ohio television markets and a chance to demonstrate loyalty to a congressional candidate, Ed Gallrein, he helped push through a primary by opposing the incumbent, said University of Kentucky political scientist Stephen Voss.

It also puts Trump within reach of another congressional district where Republicans face a tougher fight, Voss said.

Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.) is hoping to fill Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) seat, and is battling Democratic state Rep. Charles Booker. 

A Global Strategy Group poll released by Booker’s campaign Sept. 9 had him trailing 49-40, with a margin of error of 4%. McConnell, 84, has occasionally bedeviled Trump, even while pushing through his court nominees and being sidelined by health challenges. 

Barr’s Senate bid has opened up a House seat in the Lexington area, about a 90-minute drive from Trump’s rally. Democrat Zach Dembo, a former Navy JAG officer who left his job as a federal prosecutor in the Trump Justice Department, is challenging Republican Ralph Alvarado, a former state health commissioner.

The Cook Political Report moved the district Oct. 9 from “safe Republican” to the more competitive “leans Republican” category.

Republicans are favored in the state’s 4th Congressional District, where Trump helped knock off Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) in the primary, calling him a “nutjob”. Now, primary winner Ed Gallrein, a retired Navy SEAL, is taking on Democrat businesswoman Melissa Strange. Gallrein is favored, but some younger voters and indepdnents are threatening to stay home. 

“Every once in a while you see a case where the electorate is angered so much that they sit on their hands,” said Voss.

Analysts say persistent inflation, the Iran war, and fuel costs have made races competitive across the country even in Republican-leaning territory. 

Trump’s trip followed visits to Alaska, Montana, and Georgia this week.
news.summary: President Trump hits the road again Saturday in just his latest trip to rally supporters in Republican-leaning territory – this time with a trip to Kentucky, where he hopes to shore up a suddenly competitive House race and secure two other seats that have given him political heartburn.
