news.title: The $2500 Donation that could mean more for Texas' Senate race than Elon Musk’s millions
news.text:
Barbara Bush, the daughter of former President George W. Bush, has given money to a super PAC supporting Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, Houston Public Media reported.

The amount is small, but it may say something about where some Republicans stand.

Lone Star Rising PAC’s third-quarter filing with the FEC lists a $2,500 contribution from the younger Bush, dated September 23. The Bush family didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Andrew Cates, a campaign finance attorney in central Texas, noted that someone from such a prominent family could easily have given in a way that kept her name out of public view. Instead, he said, she chose a PAC that discloses all of its money, not a 501(c)(4) that would have kept her donation anonymous.

He said the sum is minor in a race that has drawn hundreds of millions of dollars.

“It’s not like Elon Musk money, obviously,” Cates said.

Still, he suggested the gift could hint at where the moderate Republican establishment is leaning and how it sees the contest ending.

Polls show Talarico and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton roughly tied, or with Talarico narrowly ahead.

Barbara Bush already made clear her willingness to back Democrats two years ago, when she supported then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election.

news.title: How Latino Voters Are Experiencing the 2026 Midterm Elections - Pew Research Center
news.text:
Several weeks out from the 2026 midterm election, Democratic congressional candidates have a sizable advantage among Latino registered voters. And while not all registered voters will cast ballots this year, Latino Democratic candidate supporters are more engaged with this year’s election compared with four years ago.

77% of Latino registered voters who support a Democratic candidate for their district in the House of Representatives say it really matters who wins control of Congress, up from 58% in 2022.

53% say they’re extremely motivated to vote, up from 41% four years ago.

45% say they’ve given a lot of thought to the upcoming elections, up from 24% in 2022.

Meanwhile, Latino voters who support Republican congressional candidates show lower levels of engagement this year compared with Latino voters supporting Democratic candidates.

Latino registered voters overall are more engaged in this year’s election than they were at a similar point before the 2022 midterms. Their current level of interest is similar to other registered voters. By contrast, in 2022, Latino voters were less engaged than other voters.

Latino voters have historically favored Democratic over Republican candidates in midterm elections, but the margin has narrowed in recent years: In 2022, Latino voters backed Democrats over Republicans by a 21 percentage point margin, down from a 47-point margin in 2018. Trump also made gains among Latino voters in presidential elections between 2016 and 2024, winning nearly half their votes two years ago. Previous Pew Research Center studies have found that differences in who turns out to vote, rather than voters switching their support between parties, have played a role in these shifts.

Two years into the second Trump administration, the president’s standing with Latino voters has deteriorated. His current job approval rating among Latino voters, at 24%, is down from 38% in February 2025. And majorities of Latino voters say the Trump administration’s policies harm Hispanics more than help them and that their situation as a group is worse than a year ago. (Jump to “Trump’s falling job approval rating among Latino registered voters.”)

The economy remains the top issue for Latino voters, who have grown more negative about economic conditions and are increasingly concerned about the cost of gas and unemployment. (Jump to “The Economy Is the Top Issue for Latino Voters in the 2026 Midterms.”)

These findings come from a new Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults, including 774 Hispanic registered voters, conducted from Sept. 28 to Oct. 4, 2026.

Vote preferences among Hispanic voters in the 2026 midterm elections

Democrats hold a 27 percentage point advantage over Republicans among all Hispanic registered voters in the national race for the House of Representatives – 51% to 24%. Another 18% say they are not sure who they would vote for, and an additional 7% indicate they would support another candidate.

According to the new survey, 65% of Hispanic voters who voted for Trump in 2024 say they support the Republican House candidate this year. Another 14% say they would vote for another candidate, 11% say they would vote for the Democratic candidate, and 10% say they’re not sure whom they would vote for.

Meanwhile, 84% of Hispanic voters who supported Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 say they back the Democratic House candidate this year.

Among those who did not vote in 2024, 47% say they would choose the Democratic candidate and 18% the Republican candidate. An additional 31% say they are unsure who they would vote for, while 4% favor another candidate.

For more information, visit the detailed tables on voting preferences and presidential approval. 

(Jump to “Latino Registered Voters See the Democratic Party More Favorably Than the Republican Party.”)

For many Latino voters, Trump is a factor in their congressional vote choices

A majority of Latino registered voters (55%) say they think of their vote for Congress this fall as a vote against Trump. Another 14% say their vote is in support of him, while 30% say he is not much of a factor.

This is a substantial change from four years ago, when 26% of Latino voters viewed their vote as support for Joe Biden and 23% viewed it as opposition to him. About half (48%) said he was not a factor in their congressional vote choice. 

Hispanic voters who back a Republican candidate are about equally likely to say their vote for Congress is a vote for Trump or that Trump is not much of a factor for their vote (46% each). Only 7% say they think about their vote as a vote against Trump.

A strong majority (84%) of Hispanic voters who say they support a Democratic candidate for Congress this year view their vote as opposition to Trump. And 14% say Trump is not a factor in their vote for Congress.

Among Hispanic voters who backed Trump in 2024, 35% say their vote for Congress this year is a vote for the president. Yet 19% view their vote as opposition to Trump. Another 46% say he is not much of a factor in their vote choice.

Trump’s falling job approval rating among Latino registered voters

Today, 24% of Latino registered voters say they approve of Trump’s handling of his job as president. This number has fallen 14 percentage points from the start of his second term, when 38% approved of his job.

The president’s job approval rating has fallen more sharply among his 2024 Hispanic voters. At the start of his second term, 93% said they approved of his job as president. Now, 57% say this – a decline of 36 percentage points. Approval has also fallen among Trump’s 2024 non-Hispanic backers, though less sharply. In February 2025, 95% approved of his job performance, compared with 68% today.

The impact of Trump’s policies on Hispanics

Seven-in-ten Hispanic registered voters (70%) say the Trump administration’s policies have been harmful to Hispanics, while 12% say they have been helpful and 16% say they have had no effect. This is similar to their assessment from a year ago, when 74% said the administration’s policies were harmful to Hispanics. 

Today, views differ sharply by how Hispanic registered voters say they will vote in the House election:

Republican candidate supporters are divided: 23% say the administration’s policies have been harmful, while 37% say they have been helpful. Another 38% say they have had no effect.

Almost all Democratic candidate supporters say the administration’s policies have been harmful to Hispanics (91%).

How Hispanic voters view the situation of Hispanics in the country

About six-in-ten Hispanic registered voters (61%) say the situation of Hispanics in the United States is worse than it was a year ago, while 11% say it is better and 26% say it is about the same.

The share who say Latinos’ situation in the U.S. is worse than a year ago is roughly the same as the share that said this a year ago (65%).

However, the reference periods differ. This year’s assessment asks respondents to compare the situation today with the first year of Trump’s second administration. Last year, they were comparing the first year of Trump’s second administration to the final year of the Biden administration.

This year’s negative assessment of Hispanics’ situation remains far above previous years: In 2021, only 28% said Hispanics’ situation had worsened in the previous year, and in 2019, 42% said this. 

Hispanic registered voters’ choice of congressional candidate this year is related to how they see the situation of U.S. Hispanics.

Hispanic Republican candidate supporters are divided: 22% say the situation of Hispanics is worse than a year ago, while 34% say it’s better and 44% say it’s about the same.

On the other hand, 79% of Democratic candidate supporters say the situation of Hispanics is worse than a year ago, while only 2% say it’s better and 19% say it’s about the same.

news.title: Atiku Fit, Ready to Traverse 36 States, FCT, ADC-PCC Declares
news.text:
Says Tinubu’s refusal to campaign nationwide is arrogant, insult to Nigerians

Accuses Kwankwaso of doing president’s bidding, describes call for former VP to step down as reckless

Chuks Okocha

The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has declared that its presidential candidate, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, is fit and ready to campaign across Nigeria’s 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory ahead of the 2027 general election.

The council also criticised President Bola Tinubu over his decision not to campaign in all states, describing it as an act of arrogance and an insult to Nigerians, while accusing former Kano State Governor Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso of advancing the president’s political interests by calling on Atiku to step down for Peter Obi.

The Director of Media and Publicity of the ADC-PCC, Kola Ologbondiyan, in a statement, was quoted to have made the remarks while receiving a delegation of youths under the aegis of Young Voters for Atiku (YVA) and in a separate response to Kwankwaso’s interview on Channels Television.

Ologbondiyan argued that a president seeking re-election should be willing to engage voters directly, account for his stewardship and present his plans for the country. He said Tinubu’s reported reluctance to campaign nationwide would give the opposition an advantage.

“What President Tinubu has done is a clear act of contempt against the Nigerian people. The APC is known for its contempt for Nigerians. How can a man who wants to be re-elected as president, after failing woefully, say he does not want to visit the people he seeks to govern?” he said.

The ADC-PCC spokesman dismissed the argument that official engagements could prevent Tinubu from campaigning across the country, citing former Presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari, as well as former United States President Donald Trump and former Vice-President Kamala Harris, as examples of political leaders who campaigned while holding or seeking public office.

He alleged that Tinubu was reluctant to face voters because of public dissatisfaction over hunger, poverty, insecurity and the state of the economy.

Ologbondiyan maintained that Atiku was physically fit, mentally alert and prepared to visit every state and the FCT to present his manifesto and seek the electorate’s mandate.

He urged Nigerians, particularly young voters, to reject the All Progressives Congress (APC) in 2027, arguing that another term for the ruling party would prolong the hardship citizens were experiencing.

He also expressed confidence that Atiku, if elected, would prioritise economic recovery, wealth creation, national security and improved living standards.

The ADC-PCC further criticised Kwankwaso for urging Atiku to step down for Obi, describing the call as reckless, self-serving and an attempt to weaken the opposition ahead of the 2027 election.

Ologbondiyan questioned why Kwankwaso was focusing on opposition leaders rather than challenging Tinubu’s administration, which the council said Nigerians were eager to vote out.

“Rather than campaigning against President Tinubu, whose administration Nigerians are eagerly working to vote out, Kwankwaso is fixated on Atiku Abubakar, the ADC candidate, whom millions of Nigerians believe can restore economic stability and make life affordable again,” he said.

He alleged that Kwankwaso’s position raised questions about his political intentions, suggesting that his actions could benefit the ruling APC by creating divisions among opposition parties.

“What Kwankwaso is doing amounts to advancing President Tinubu’s interests. It is a familiar APC strategy to use willing collaborators within the opposition to create confusion, sow division and weaken the collective efforts to bring about political change,” Ologbondiyan said.

He also argued that Kwankwaso’s political influence in Kano should not be considered indispensable to any presidential candidate seeking victory in the state. Citing the 2003 and 2007 presidential elections, he said former President Muhammadu Buhari had secured victories in Kano without Kwankwaso’s support, adding that Atiku could also win the state in 2027.

Ologbondiyan further questioned Kwankwaso’s ability to translate his regional influence into nationwide electoral support, citing his fourth-place finish in the 2023 presidential election.

He also alleged that Kwankwaso’s call for Obi’s candidacy was driven partly by personal political ambition and possible calculations ahead of the 2031 election.

The ADC-PCC director maintained that Atiku had built political relationships across Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones over more than three decades, which he said positioned the former vice-president to assemble a broad national coalition.

He urged Kwankwaso and other opposition figures to support Atiku, arguing that opposition leaders should prioritise defeating the APC rather than undermining one another.

“The task before opposition leaders is not to undermine one another for personal political advantage but to unite around the urgent national mission of rescuing Nigeria,” Ologbondiyan said.

The council also claimed that it had been politically strengthened by the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, saying the event had not attracted endorsements from ADC members or sympathisers.

news.title: Give Us Your $$$$$
news.text:
by W.D. Ehrhart

Holy cow! I’ve just gotten a personal message from the world-famous political consultant James Carville. It says so right on the envelope: “A Personal Message from James Carville.” And not just personal, but confidential, too. Right there above my name on the envelope, it says “PERSONAL & CONFIDENTIAL.” Imagine that.

But inside is a printed notice that begins “Dear William.” Nobody ever calls me “William” except for receptionists in medical offices or stuff like that. Absolutely nothing “personal” about it. The entire document has been mechanically produced, virtually untouched by human hands, James Carville’s or anyone else’s.

Golly gee. Was I ever disappointed.

Well, no, not really. But I do wonder how gullible and naïve the Democrats think I am that they insult me by trying to claim this appeal for my $$$$$ is anything other than what it is: a mass mailing to millions of people who have somehow or other ended up on Democratic mailing lists.

I need to say here that I will only mention the Republican party in passing. I am 78 years old, and have never missed an election in which I was eligible to vote: general, primary, or special. And in all those elections, I have never voted for a Republican. I expect nothing from Republicans, and they have never failed to meet my expectations.

But over the years, I have often voted for Democrats because given the choices I’ve had, well, what choice did I have?

Not until 2016, however, did I ever make a financial donation to a political candidate because no candidate ever even came close to reflecting my own political beliefs.

But that changed when Bernie Sanders took a run at the Democratic nomination for the presidency. I’d been following Sanders’s career ever since he was elected mayor of Burlington, Vermont, in 1981 as an “Independent” (actually, a Socialist). I began contributing to his campaign monthly, and did so right up until the Democratic party establishment elite screwed him out of the nomination in favor of the unlikeable and unelectable Hilary Clinton.

I should have learned my lesson, but I didn’t. I contributed to Joe Biden’s campaign in 2020. He was elected to do one thing: remove Donald Trump from the political stage, preferably by putting him behind bars where he belongs. But Biden failed to accomplish that. Failed miserably as it turns out.

In 2022, I contributed to John Fetterman’s senate campaign. You can see what I got for my $$$$$ with that guy. And two years later, I contributed to the reelection campaign of Pennsylvania Senator Bob Casey, Jr., who ran such a lackluster campaign that he couldn’t manage to beat a carpetbagger from Connecticut. I gave $$$$$ to the Kamala Harris campaign.

And apparently my having contributed anything to any Democratic candidate has resulted in opening the floodgates. I am now being bombarded with desperate appeals from all over these United States: Georgia, Ohio, Florida, Alaska, Michigan, Texas. The envelope in which I’m supposed to send my donation to Amy Klobuchar is addressed to “Minnesotans for Klobuchar,” though I am not a Minnesotan for Klobuchar or even a Minnesotan at all. (At least her letter begins “Dear Friend” rather than “Dear William.”)

My governor, Josh Shapiro, sends me letter after letter—at least one every other week—warning of dire consequences if he is not reelected. Last time I checked, a few weeks ago, Shapiro had $38,300,000 available in his campaign “war chest”; his opponent had $956,000. Look carefully at those numbers. Shapiro ought to be ashamed of himself for continuing to claim that he needs my $$$$$ or his campaign is doomed.

I understand that political campaigns cost $$$$$, especially since our Supremely Unjust Court has eliminated any restrictions on $$$$$ in politics. And I realize that the Uber-rich are pumping millions and millions and millions of dollars into Republican campaigns.

But I also remember last June 2025 when I was out in the street with millions of ordinary Americans participating in the NO KINGS protests while Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries, Nancy Pelosi, Kamala Harris, and the Clintons were eating Wagyu beef and truffle agnolotti at the mindbogglingly lavish estate of George Soros.

How much did that cost? How much do these millions of mailings cost (nevermind all those trees destroyed to make the paper)? How much do the text messages I receive by the dozens and scores cost? How much do the same tired old TV campaign ads I see year after year—about as creative and inspiring as a wad of used chewing gum—how much do those cost, and how effective are they?

Do all these candidates from hither and yon, almost none of whom I can even vote for myself, think that I’m eating Wagyu beef and truffle agnolotti?

I just got a letter today from Barack Obama. The envelope says “Presidential correspondence enclosed for William Ehrhart.” Wow. I’m flattered. A letter from the president. Well, the former president at least. And guess what? He wants my $$$$$.

W.D. Ehrhart is a retired Master Teacher of History & English, and author of a Vietnam War memoir trilogy published by McFarland.

news.title: Trump’s ‘most-feared man in government’ torched by his own old ‘chilling’ warning: analyst
news.text:
President Donald Trump's top communications regulator is being haunted by words he wrote just a few years ago.

In a column published Friday by The Bulwark, critic Sonny Bunch zeroed in on a February 2021 statement from Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr condemning Democrats for sending letters to cable providers and other regulated companies that carried certain news outlets.

At the time, Carr warned those companies were being told they "will pay a price" if the targeted newsrooms didn't fall in line, calling it "a chilling transgression of the free speech rights that every media outlet in this country enjoys."

Bunch argued Carr has since become exactly what he once denounced, describing him as "one of President Trump's favored tools of government interference in day-to-day life" who leaps into action whenever the president wants a critic silenced.

Trump appeared to relish that reputation at a campaign rally in Alaska earlier this week, where he gave Carr a chuckling introduction. "And we have the FCC head, the most-feared man in government here, Brendan," Trump said. "Thank you, Brendan, what the hell are you doing here?"

Bunch pointed to a string of moves he said reflect that role. CBS parent Paramount agreed to pay $16 million toward Trump's future presidential library to settle the president's lawsuit over a "60 Minutes" interview with Kamala Harris, after Carr signaled the dispute could hold up its merger with Skydance. Carr approved the deal soon after.

ABC's Jimmy Kimmel was yanked off the air hours after Carr warned "we can do this the easy way or the hard way" over a joke about Charlie Kirk's assassination. And Carr is reportedly probing ABC News' website, even though the FCC has no authority over online news.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez told Bunch the agency has abandoned its independence. "The FCC has become a political arm of the administration," she said. "Prior to this administration, our decisions were based on technical expertise and policy concerns, not the political whims of the White House."

Bunch contrasted Carr with Ajit Pai, who led the FCC during Trump's first term and declared in 2017 that the agency "does not have the authority to revoke a license of a broadcast station based on the content of a particular newscast."

The hypocrisy, Bunch wrote, isn't even the worst of it. Concentrating that much power in one man's hands, he argued, is "antithetical to freedom of expression," and he predicted little will change without serious oversight from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

news.title: Trump ties, fraud crisis put Tafoya and Flanagan on defense in Senate debate
news.text:
Republican Michele Tafoya sought to establish her independence from President Donald Trump, while Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan faced questions about party loyalty and her responsibility for Minnesota’s fraud crisis during their first and only scheduled U.S. Senate debate Friday.

The debate came just days after Trump encouraged Minnesotans to vote for Tafoya. Flanagan used the event to cast the former sportscaster as someone who would be a rubber stamp for the president’s agenda. 

“Let’s be clear: Donald Trump doesn’t just endorse anybody. In fact, he endorses against people in his own party if they dare to take him on,” Flanagan said. “Michele Tafoya passed his litmus test with flying colors.” 

But Tafoya used the debate to highlight where she would break from her party and Trump, including on the Iran war. She also sought to turn the tables on Flanagan’s critique.

“I would challenge my opponent to tell us where and when she has ever parted with her own party, with the far left flank of her party, on any issue,” Tafoya said. 

Tafoya kept a distance from Trump throughout the debate and declined to say whether she wanted his endorsement or would campaign alongside him in Minnesota.

“My campaign is about including people from all along the political spectrum,” she said. “I invite Trump voters. I invite Kamala Harris voters.” 

Flanagan similarly declined to say whether she wanted Gov. Tim Walz to campaign with her as Republicans made his administration’s fraud crisis a central attack.

news.title: Nobody Wants To Be the Pro-Tech Candidate in This New York Race That Could Flip the House
news.text:
The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates running for the House of Representatives and endorsed by NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani are all but guaranteed to win their general elections this November, but that does not mean the midterm drama is over in New York. In the state's 17th congressional district, which includes the lower Hudson Valley, Democratic challenger Cait Conley, a combat veteran who served on the Biden administration's National Security Council, could unseat incumbent Republican congressman Mike Lawler in one of the most consequential races of the midterms. 

The highly contested purple district voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election while reelecting Lawler for his second term. Now, Lawler is attempting to win a third term as support for President Donald Trump wanes ahead of the midterms. As of Friday, The Cook Political Report lists the race, which could determine control of the House, as a toss-up. 

If elected, Conley would have far more in common with the "Badass Women" coalition of security state and military veterans than with DSA types (think more Sen. Elissa Slotkin from Michigan than Darializa Avila Chevalier). As Judge Street Journal's Timmy Facciola notes, "Conley's candidacy is testing the viability of a tactful centrism that rebukes left-wing positions like abolishing ICE or restricting weapon shipments to Israel." Lawler is also vying for moderates, pitching himself as "one of the most bipartisan members of Congress" and emphasizing his willingness to break with Trump occasionally while still welcoming Trump's support. 

While Lawler and Conley certainly are not pure MAGA acolytes or DSA members, both have leaned into a tech-critical position, much like that of more radical populists like Lina Khan or Steve Bannon, revealing how pervasive anti-tech sentiment has become in mainstream politics. 

This tech skepticism was on full display during an October 14 debate, when each candidate made the case for why they were the most equipped to regulate AI, insisting that the industry needs guardrails. 

Conley said members of Congress do not want to regulate AI because "they want to look out for their billionaire and trillionaire backers like Elon Musk, who is pouring over $260 million into this midterm election." She then added that Musk backed Lawler in his 2024 race. 

Lawler then accused Conley, who previously consulted for Primer AI, of being "the AI candidate for the AI industry."

While Lawler and Conley disagree on specific data center regulations (Conley supports Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul's data center moratorium while Lawler supports local zoning control over data centers), neither wants to pitch themselves as an explicitly pro-data center candidate. During the debate, Conley claimed that, "On Mike Lawler's watch there have been five data centers built in Rockland County." Lawler has said that he had no say in the decision to build the data centers, and during the debate, he pointed out that the facilities were built for financial services. Lawler also attempted to attack Conley over data centers, slamming her in an ad for saying "we need data centers." Regardless of the candidates' specific policies on data centers, their attacks on one another demonstrate that cheerleading hyperscale data center development is a political liability. In their district, data center has presumably become a dirty term. 

The candidates' tech-skeptical rhetoric did not end with unchecked data center development. After the debate, Reason asked both candidates about their positions on age-verification laws for social media and AI, since such regulations raise significant privacy and censorship concerns by age-gating the internet. Unsurprisingly, both Lawler, who voted for the controversial KIDS Act, and Conley, who has proposed stricter age verification for AI tools, parroted platitudes about why such online safety regulations are necessary to protect children. 

"We have watched how social media is literally hurting the mental health of children," Conley told Reason. "And when you talk about the power of AI and what that power could do, we have to regulate this." 

Lawler gave a similar response, telling Reason that he respects free speech but that protecting children "is paramount." 

This bipartisan consensus over social media regulation has long been brewing in Congress. The mainstream political conversations about AI and data centers, however, are relatively new this midterm election cycle. And it appears both Lawler and Conley have figured out which way Americans' sentiment toward AI is leaning, and they have waged their campaigns accordingly.
news.summary: Republican incumbent Mike Lawler and Democratic challenger Cait Conley are trying to tie each other to the AI industry and data centers.
news.author: Meagan O'Rourke

news.title: Map Shows 14 GOP-Held House Seats Shifting Toward Democrats in Past Week
news.text: Republicans have been dealt another blow as data compiled from the Cook Political Report shows 14 U.S. House seats in 10 states currently held by Republicans are shifting toward Democrats 18 days before the November 3 midterm elections. Republicans are fighting to defend their razor-thin majorities in both chambers of Congress as voters weigh concerns about the economy, inflation, President Donald Trump's job performance and the ongoing U.S. war with Iran. The GOP currently holds a 218-214 edge in the House and a 53-47 majority in the Senate, leaving little room for losses in a midterm cycle that features a number of highly competitive races. Democrats have an opportunity to flip one or both chambers, including in several states that have traditionally leaned Republican. "Republicans remain laser-focused on winning, protecting and expanding President Trump’s House majority," Republican National Committee Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre told Newsweek. "While Democrats celebrate political ratings, we’re thinking outside the box and pouring resources into battleground districts to highlight President Trump’s historic achievements, boost our candidates and defy history on November 3.” Newsweek reached out to the Democratic National Committee by email and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee by phone for comment on Friday. Which House Races Are Shifting Democrat? On Friday, a Cook Political Report said that 11 House races are shifting toward Democrats, including five seats in four states held by Republicans. Of the five, all are still considered "lean R," according to Cook, but the move indicates that the results could be tighter than originally thought. Similarly, a report on October 9 showed nine House seats currently held by Republicans shifting toward Democrats, including traditionally Republican states that Trump won big in 2024. Despite the changes, several of the impacted states are still favored to have a Republican win. Minnesota Minnesota's First Congressional District, represented by Republican Brad Finstad, has shifted from "likely R" to "lean R." Finstad is facing Democrat Jake Johnson, with some polls showing the candidates tied. Trump won Finstad's district by 12 points in 2024. Ohio Ohio has two House seats occupied by Republicans—Mike Turner in the 10th District and Mike Carey in the 15th—that shifted from "likely R" to "lean R" this week. Turner is running against Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, while Carey is up against Democrat Don Leonard. Trump won Ohio by nearly 12 points in 2024. When it comes to the Senate, the race between Republican Senator Jon Husted and Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown is among a handful of toss-ups that could determine the balance of power. Kansas Kansas' 2nd Congressional District, represented by Republican Derek Schmidt, shifted from "solid R" to "likely R." The Democratic candidate is Don Coover. Trump won the district by 20 points in 2024. Nebraska Nebraska's 1st Congressional District seat, occupied by Republican Mike Flood, shifted from "solid R" to "likely R." The Democratic candidate is Chris Backemeyer. Trump won Nebraska by 20 points in 2024. Iowa Republicans Mariannette Miller-Meeks in the 1st district and Zach Nunn in the 3rd saw their races shift from "toss-up" to "lean D." In the 1st district, the Democratic candidate is Christina Bohannan, while Sarah Trone Garriott is running in the 3rd. Trump won Iowa for all three of his presidential campaigns, including by nearly 14 points in 2024. Iowa is also among the most competitive U.S. Senate races, with Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek vying for retiring Republican Joni Ernst's seat. Pennsylvania Three of Pennsylvania's House seats currently occupied by Republicans showed changes as well. The races for the 7th and 10th congressional districts, held by Ryan Mackenzie and Scott Perry, respectively, were change from "toss-up" to "lean D" by Cook. The 1st Congressional District, held by Republican Brian Fitzpatrick, shifted from "likely R" to "lean R." Democrats running are: Bob Brooks (in the 7th District); Janelle Stelson, who is currently leading Perry in polls in the 10th; and Bucks County Commissioner Bob Harvie in the 1st. Trump won Pennsylvania by less than 2 points in 2024. Michigan Michigan's 4th Congressional District, held by Republican Bill Huizenga, moved from "lean R" to "toss-up" category. The Democratic candidate is state Senator Sean McCann. Trump won Michigan by 1.4 points in 2024. Michigan is also tight in the Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, to succeed retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. Virginia Virginia's 1st Congressional District, a seat held by Republican Rob Wittman, shifted from "lean R" to "toss-up." Democrat Shannon Taylor led Wittman by 4 points in a recent Washington Post poll. Trump lost Virginia to Kamala Harris by 5 points in 2024. Arkansas Arkansas' 2nd Congressional District, held by Republican French Hill, shifted from "solid R" to "likely R." The Democratic candidate is Chris Jones, a nuclear engineer who ran for governor in 2022. Trump won Arkansas by more than 30 points in 2024. Indiana Indiana's 5th Congressional District, held by Republican Victoria Spartz, shifted from "solid R" to "likely R." Spartz's Democratic opponent is state Senator JD Ford. Trump won Indiana by 19 points in 2024. What Happens Next In most states, early voting has begun and will continue up until Election Day on November 3. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Skinner and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: More than a dozen U.S. House seats in 10 states currently held by Republicans are shifting toward Democrats.

news.title: “History Will Judge”: Fox News Anchor Bret Baier on Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth’s War With the Press
news.text:
Tonight he’s on better behavior, waving off wine and sticking to soda water. “I have an election diet,” he tells me, explaining that he drops around 15 pounds every October of an election year. He recommends the beef tenderloin but orders the branzino for himself.
Tucked into a corner seat at the best table in the room, Baier is in his element. He pats down his hair, which is short and sculpted and appears totally immovable, like the top of a Playmobil figurine. He’s just come off set, and his face remains brushed with the tan makeup that ensures its uniformity and consistency through time and space and episodes of Special Report, the daily news program he has anchored for the last 17 years. The job—that is, serving as the face of the mighty conservative network’s news operation, which is celebrating its 30th year in business this month—has grown more challenging over the years as the institution has become increasingly intertwined with Donald Trump’s political movement.
We’re discussing the president’s attacks on the press, which recently culminated in an unprecedented attempt to ban certain news outlets from the White House over their coverage. “We made our feelings clear the second it happened,” Baier tells me. Privately, Baier lobbied Trump to reverse the ban, I’d been told by a source with knowledge of the conversations. Publicly, Fox News joined the rest of the media in pulling its coverage from the White House press pool. “There are die-hard MAGA folks who say that it was the wrong move, but there was no doubt,” he says. “There was never even a split second of thinking about it.”
It isn’t the only measure Fox is taking against the Trump administration: Internally, the network has for months paused booking interviews with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a former Fox News host, following his ejection of journalists from the Pentagon. “I always had a good relationship with him at Fox,” Baier says of Hegseth. “Obviously, I’m not a proponent of what he did with the Pentagon press pool. And I see…[the president] talks about him all the time as central casting.”
I ask whether he would host Hegseth on Special Report. “If I get clearance to, I would,” he says. He’s not getting clearance right now? “No, I mean, I think we made another decision as a news organization once we left the premises and got kicked out, and that was the decision that was made.”
It’s an early taste of the anchorman’s studied posture of neutrality—though Baier does, for a moment, betray a point of view. “I hope he lets the press back in,” he says.
“I hate the tie,” he says.
“I know you hate the tie,” the producer responds.
In his second decade as anchor and executive editor, Baier has perfected the science of Special Report, Fox’s flagship news operation, which airs weekdays at 6 p.m. and is run with a fierce efficiency. There are around three crew members on set at any given time, and another 10 staffers sit in a control room, a whirring hub managing a network of foreign and domestic correspondents who beam in for quick hits.
“Honestly, I hate the tie,” Baier says, fixated. “It screws up the tie.”
The microphone remains on the tie. A producer begins the countdown to live, and at exactly 6 p.m., Baier looks up from his laptop for the first time since sitting down and says amiably into the camera: “Good evening, and welcome to Washington. I’m Bret Baier.”
In the first block of the show, he throws to a correspondent in Paris covering the riots there, then to the State Department, the White House, and Ithaca, New York, for a dispatch on the protests at Cornell University. In 10 minutes, Special Report has covered five stories. In a final segment, a panel featuring three national political reporters weighs in on the upcoming midterms. By the end, this precisely choreographed endeavor produces an hour of television that draws an average of more than 2.5 million viewers each night, which makes Special Report the most watched hard-news program in all of cable.
These days, Baier measures his success against that of the broadcast networks—CBS, ABC, NBC—which he beats in some key markets. But he remembers when his ambitions were considerably more modest. “I went around doing stories and I’d say I was with Fox, and they’d say, ‘Is that the Simpsons network?’” he says. “And so the prospect of us beating a big [broadcast] network that still has much further reach is really pretty amazing.”
Seventeen years and a few dollars later, Baier now divides his time between Washington, where he still spends three to four nights a week, and a large home he recently purchased in Palm Beach, a short drive from Mar-a-Lago. He sold his house in the capital, a mansion in leafy Foxhall inspired by a Loire Valley château, to Howard Lutnick, Trump’s billionaire commerce secretary. “He got a good deal,” Baier says.
Baier’s rise to television stardom began by violent chance. He was an industrious correspondent in Fox’s Atlanta bureau when the first plane hit the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001, and he was called to the network’s New York City headquarters to help cover the attack. “We started driving, and then the third plane hit the Pentagon,” he says. “They rerouted us.” He drove from Georgia to Arlington, Virginia. “I started doing live shots for Fox affiliates outside the burning Pentagon that night, and I never left.” He was soon named Fox’s Pentagon correspondent, traveling frequently to Iraq and Afghanistan. In 2009 he took over Special Report from his mentor, Brit Hume, who offered three simple pieces of advice to the young newsman: “The show is not about you, the show is not about you, and let the news drive the show.”
Back then, Baier faced stiff competition within the network from straight-news anchors like Chris Wallace and Shepard Smith. But Trump’s rise to power ushered in changes at Fox News, which has seen the news hours on its schedule shrink, replaced by opinion shows, which tend to draw stronger ratings. “The landscape changed,” Baier says. “There’s a lot more opinion programming overall in the cable universe.” In this uncertain new world, Baier has established himself as the face of Fox’s news operation, the man called upon to moderate presidential debates and interview world leaders.
When it comes to foreign heads of state, it can sometimes feel like Special Report is their first stop in Washington. “I’d like to say it’s because the booking is really good,” Baier says with a laugh. “When you have big foreign leaders appear one after another, they line up like planes at Dulles.” There’s also the matter of who’s watching. “I hear they also want to talk to a viewer, a particular one who watches Special Report,” Baier adds. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, amid a yearslong bid to convince Trump to support his cause, has appeared seven times.
Special Report’s most important viewer has a fraught relationship with the show and its host. Trump has lashed out at Baier before, calling him “nasty” after the Fox anchor pointed out in an interview that Trump lost the 2020 election. But Baier maintains a good relationship with the president, who often calls to talk off the record, sometimes to complain. Baier recalls one example, deploying a perfect Trump impression: “‘Bret, I tell you what, you’re a six. You’re not a seven or an eight. You’re a six.’” Baier says he replied, “I’ll take six. I’m pretty close to five. I’m doing good.”
During a book party that Baier hosted for Sylvester Stallone earlier this month, he pulled his phone out and said there was someone who wanted to talk to the actor. It was Trump, who had called to offer well-wishes. The anchor and the president have also golfed together, which critics say betrays a coziness between the scandal-plagued president and the newsman. “Look, if you had three hours with the leader of the free world where you could pick his brain off the record while you’re playing a sport,” Baier says, “I would take that with any president.”
Yet Baier’s critics question his claim to impartiality—citing, beyond the network’s overall reputation, a few high-profile incidents. In 2016 he issued a correction and an apology after inaccurately reporting, days before the election, that Hillary Clinton would be indicted. And during the 2024 campaign, Baier interrogated Vice President Kamala Harris in a manner some viewers found aggressive, with the host interrupting her at points—though Baier would later contend that Harris came into the interview looking for a fight.
Like any anchor, Baier is determined to give little away, and he carries a politico’s devotion to staying on message. When he’s questioned about the other activities of the network that employs him, he says he maintains “horse blinders” on his show. This is not entirely true, of course. He follows the controversies and outrages and scandals provoked (and stoked) by the rest of the network and has privately expressed frustrations with some of its coverage, according to one person who knows him personally. In 2020, as some Fox hosts promoted Trump’s false claims about the election, Baier fumed about the coverage on Maria Bartiromo’s show, according to internal communications revealed as part of a lawsuit at the time. He does not share any of this with me.
“Friends with Maria,” he says when I ask about her abrupt ouster from the network over the summer. “Great lady. Didn’t have any specifics when it all went down. Still really don’t have the whole picture”—and then we’re interrupted by the Trump adviser Jason Miller, who has come over to say hello.
When I continue my questioning about his Fox colleagues and reach Mark Levin, the cantankerous windbag who recently defended Trump’s media ban even as the rest of the network fought against it, Baier demurs again. “Again, my day is with literally horse blinders on from six to seven,” he says.
“But you don’t really have horse blinders on,” I note. “You watch this stuff.”
“I don’t actually watch it,” he says. “But obviously I see clips and I hear it. Does it bother me? No, because you know what? There’s an opinion page and a news page. They’re opinion folks. They do a great job at what they do. We’re rowing the same way for the company, but it’s a different job.”
This zone defense has been honed through years of sitting with journalists like me, answering questions like this. “Do you ask this question to NBC when they go crazy on their opinion programs?” he asks. I assure him that I would. “Fox is under the spotlight a lot, and always has been,” he continues. “I get asked about opinion folks all the time, and I’m fine with it. I don’t see a lot of stories that scrutinize what the opinion people on other channels are saying.”
The Trump era is different, of course. The false information the president demands his supporters endorse is of a magnitude not seen in modern times—a reality well-known to Fox given the costly defamation lawsuits the network faced over Trump’s election lies. Amid the 2020 chaos, Baier fact-checked false claims about the election on his show. But as the network faced a viewer revolt over its election desk’s call that Joe Biden won the state of Arizona, he reportedly suggested that the network “pull” the call and “put it back in [Trump’s] column.” (In a statement at the time, Baier said his comments were taken out of context. Some analysts, including Nate Silver, had argued Fox should retract their call—which ended up being correct.) Baier’s sign-off on Special Report is “Fair, balanced, and unafraid,” but that motto sounds more strained than ever in a time with rampant misinformation and growing audience pressures, not to mention a press corps treated with hostility and distance.
When Baier introduced the report on the riots in France this month, he accurately described them as student protests against poor conditions in public schools. But he also said that Trump “is blaming Islam and unchecked immigration” for the unrest. What the audience did not hear is that there is no basis whatsoever for the president’s claim. Is there not some obligation for the newsman to inform his viewers, I ask him, when one side of the story he’s relaying is false?
Baier says that he often does push back on false information from Republicans. In recent interviews, he pressed Trump on his past claim that the Iran war would be “fairly quick” and Bessent on the president’s dreadful approval ratings. He describes his role these days as that of a hockey goalie, blocking whatever bad information he can from reaching the back of the net. But the balance doctrine also creates an uncomfortable obligation to host Trump’s breathless defenders on Special Report.
Take the case of Mollie Hemingway, a pundit who once blasted Trump as a “demagogue” but now plays the part of Trump booster on Baier’s show, amplifying his conspiracy theories about elections and more. (She went so far as to write a book about the 2020 election called Rigged.) Is there any point at which Baier considers whether someone like Hemingway should continue to be on air? He pauses for a while.
“I’m still the goalie,” he says. “If Mollie said something that was egregious on the panel, I would step in and confront. But to hear where the Trump administration stands or what they’re thinking, I think is actually valuable in the discussion.” Special Report often pairs these pro-Trump voices with liberal pundits like Jessica Tarlov and Leslie Marshall, and its Common Ground segment brings together lawmakers from both sides of the aisle.
But the view that Trump’s side should be thoroughly represented shapes much of what airs on Special Report. That might come down to earnest belief, or survival instinct. (The newsmen who faced the wrath of the Fox audience after expressing too much skepticism of Trump could fill Cafe Milano.) “I think history will judge whether he’s been, in the big picture, this great figure or whether he has been what some would describe as a divisive figure,” Baier says. “But Donald Trump will be a consequential president in history’s mind. And how you read it will be what point of view you come from.”
One wonders how Baier would judge the history we’re living through. He’s written nine books, all New York Times bestsellers, including six about American presidents. His latest, The Case for America, is a paean to the founding ideals of the country. In the introduction, Baier outlines several “bedrock principles” that defined the founding of the United States: freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom of religion, and the peaceful transfer of power. I point out that Trump in many ways represents the antithesis of those principles—between the 2020 election crisis, his attempted “Muslim ban,” his crackdown on the press, the legal harassment of his critics… There’s too much to list over a two-course dinner. Did that come to mind as he was writing the book?
“It wasn’t specifically written like that,” Baier says. “But it was specific to look back at what’s important to the founders and what they believe. So if you take that away from that, that’s fine.” He adds: “I think there are a lot of Trump people who would push back at some of your characterizations about lack of freedom for religion.”
Did Trump not run on banning Muslims from the United States?
“It didn’t last long,” Baier says, apparently reassured by the judicial limitations placed on Trump’s crusade. I ask about the threats to the American project that his book warns against—extremism, venality, hyperpartisan coarseness. Is Trump not the primary culprit driving those trends? The day prior, I point out, the president called Annie Andrews, the Democratic US Senate candidate in South Carolina, “Trannie Andrews.”
Baier pauses. “Some of the rhetoric is quite something,” he says. “But it’s all part of the story. Clearly, Donald Trump hasn’t done the ‘common ground’ part of my book as well as anybody else. But he got elected by the population in this country, and so he’s the president of the United States.”
What does that afford him? A pass on some of this?
“Not a pass. We definitely have to cover it and have on the critics of how he operates, but also listen to the administration’s side, because what Donald Trump says is one thing, and things that he does are another thing.”
Earlier that evening, as a black car carries us from the Fox bureau to Milano, Baier is reminiscing about his long career in Washington. We pass the Kennedy Center, an institution he once frequented as a crystal-clinking veteran of the capital’s cocktail party circuit, and I ask what he makes of Trump’s hostile takeover and subsequent destruction of the arts center.
He pauses. “It’s a fascinating story,” he says.
I try again. The scaffolding hiding Trump’s foiled attempt to add his name to the memorial is interesting, isn’t it?
“It’s a fascinating story,” he says again.

news.title: Trump endorses Tafoya in closely watched Minnesota U.S. Senate race
news.text:
(The Center Square) – President Donald Trump has endorsed Republican and former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya in Minnesota’s U.S. Senate race.

“You have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who is a very respected person,” Trump said during a rally in Ohio on Monday. “It’s hard to win because they cheat in their elections. I thought I won Minnesota three times.”

This endorsement comes just three weeks until Election Day.

Tafoya, who is running against Democrat Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, has since downplayed the endorsement, saying she “heard about that.”

“This campaign is about bringing all Minnesotans together whether they voted for President Trump or whether they voted for Kamala Harris,” Tafoya added.

That hasn’t stopped Flanagan’s campaign from using the endorsement to criticize Tafoya, saying she is “lockstep with Trump’s MAGA agenda.”

“Donald Trump wants you to vote for Michele Tafoya,” Flanagan said. “I'm asking you to vote for the future Minnesotans deserve—one without Trump's chaos and cruelty. That's the choice in this race.”

Tafoya and Flanagan are neck and neck in the most-recent polling of Minnesota’s U.S. Senate race.

Flanagan currently leads Tafoya 44.8% to 43.3%, according to the average of the four most-recent polls compiled by 270toWin. That is well within the margin of error.

According to the Cook Political Report, the Minnesota U.S. Senate race is predicted to be likely Democrat. It is expected to be one of the bellwether races set to determine the balance of congressional power.

Of the 100 seats in the U.S. Senate, 33 are up for regular election in 2026, along with two special elections. Democrats currently hold 13 of the seats on the ballot, while Republicans hold 22. That means this election cycle will determine which party controls the 120th Congress.

A Republican candidate has not won a U.S. Senate seat in Minnesota since 2002. Tafoya hopes to be the first, labeling herself a political outsider.

“Minnesotans are rejecting Peggy Flanagan’s record of failure,” she said. “Gang violence. Rampant fraud. Declining test scores. All on her watch as lieutenant governor. It’s time for an outsider.”

Flanagan, who has served alongside Gov. Tim Walz since 2018, is running amid ongoing concerns over fraud in the state.

“Peggy Flanagan stood beside Tim Walz for eight years while Minnesota suffered billions in taxpayer dollars lost to fraud, a free-fall in academic performance, and rising crime,” Tafoya said. “Now she wants a promotion to the U.S. Senate. Eight years of failure doesn’t deserve a promotion.”

Flanagan has called out Tafoya for supporting President Donald Trump, calling her a “yes vote” for him if elected.

“We have a choice, Minnesota,” Flanagan said. “Do you want a Senator who will work for you to lower costs, end the illegal war in Iran, and hold ICE accountable? Or do you want another Senator for Trump?”

Election Day is 18 days away, but absentee ballots have already been distributed statewide, and early voting begins today.
news.summary: (The Center Square) – President Donald Trump has endorsed Republican and former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya in Minnesota’s U.S. Senate race.

news.title: MEAN GIRLS: 'View' crew preaches girl power ... unless you're Republican
news.text:
“The View” crew blew a gasket over Shane Gillis’ “Saturday Night Live” monologue mocking scantily clad gym gals. At the same time, they dabbled in actual misogyny.

Even by “View” standards, it was peak hypocrisy.

Biden, the actor said weeks before the president melted down during his final debate, was 'sharp as a tack.'

The hosts trashed Katie Zacharia, who by most accounts had a rough debut as the new press secretary. She’s a Republican, so she’s fair game to “The View.” And that’s fine. We expect the show’s partisanship to trump any “girl power” collegiality.

It’s baked into the nutty cake.

Except the hosts suggested that Zacharia slept her way into the position. Co-host Alyssa Farrah Griffin asked how she “got through the door” to become the new press secretary.

“I’ll tell ya how she got through the door,” Sara Haines said, sparking laughs from the oh-so-feminist crowd and co-hosts.

Titter-titter. Chuckle-chuckle. What’s more empowering than women insisting other women got work through sexual favors sans proof? Let’s hope Gillis doesn’t riff on Kamala Harris’ early days in politics. He might get canceled yet again …

Conspiracy bleary

The truth is out there, but you’ll need a Hulu subscription to find it.

Director Ryan Coogler’s “X-Files” reboot landed on the streamer this week. The project stars Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel, taking over for Gillian Anderson and David Duchovny. The actors play entirely new characters in the series, but it looks like Mulder and Scully will make appearances along the way.

Imagine the new conspiracies the show can tackle! The government spreads massive lies about a China-born infection … a foreign country teams with a political rebel to win an election … a U.S. president’s cognitive decline is hidden for four straight years.

Or the show could bring in the son of the Smoking Man. We’ll see …

Did he stutter?

Well, that was awkward.

Michael Douglas has done it all in his 82 years, at least from a Hollywood perspective. Oscars. Acclaim. Nepo baby-ism. What a life.

What hasn’t he done? Sit with someone willing to debunk his boilerplate Democrat views. He got that chance, finally, when Joe Rogan read him, and his audience, the riot act on progressives gone wild.

An open border? No honest primaries for year after year? And, most specifically, they covered up for a president who clearly had some form of dementia.

You know the thing.

Rogan was on a roll, but the most awkward element of their exchange dealt with Biden’s obvious decline. Why? It wasn’t long ago when Douglas was part of the Biden cover-up.

Biden, the actor said weeks before the president melted down during his final debate, was “sharp as a tack.” Douglas even cited Biden’s “stutter” excuse that mysteriously appeared over the past few years after decades in D.C.

Douglas appears to be legitimately “sharp as a tack,” thank goodness. Let’s hope he took away some lessons from the exchange …

Laugh track

Chuck Lorre blames a Hollywood writers' strike for the end of democracy.

He framed it that way in his new book, a memoir called “Sitcom.” After all, Lorre has made more than a few modern classics, from “The Big Bang Theory” to “Two and a Half Men.”

Credit where credit is due.

The far-Left Deadline.com pressed Lorre on that hyperbolic phrasing, tied to the 2007-2008 WGA strike that helped spark a crush of new reality showcases.

Like “The Apprentice,” starring Donald Trump, he insinuated. Except Lorre might be bad at math, since “The Apprentice” debuted in 2004.

The strike, he said, “brought about these enormously profitable, cheap-to-produce reality shows … and that ultimately led to a show like 'The Apprentice,' which probably would never have seen the light of day had it not been for that.”

Who knew a reality show could end the greatest nation on earth?

 Either way, Lorre could ask Young Sheldon for help on his math skills …

What the world doesn’t need is another John Oliver. One is one too many, culturally speaking. But former NBA star Blake Griffin sees the far-left HBO host as a model, of sorts, for his new sports-themed late-night show.

“The Stepback with Blake Griffin” soon bows on Amazon and YouTube, with Griffin hailing Oliver as his role model.

The funniest part? Someone thinking late-night TV is the future and itching for a seat at the table.

news.title: Young voters who backed Trump voice regret ahead of midterms
news.text:
For Remi Martinez, it’s the deportations. For Michael Johnson, it’s the economy. For Suzanna Bridges, it’s the Epstein files and what she sees as misogyny embedded in the culture of the Trump administration.

All three youthful Americans voted for President Donald Trump two years ago. All three regret it. All say they will vote Democratic this year, or not at all.

“I can’t go red, not this time — no,” said Johnson, 26, a sales representative for a plastics company in Des Moines, Iowa.

In 2024, more than half of young men — 55% — supported Trump, according to an analysis of New York Times/Siena University polling, a dramatic departure from past elections when young Americans largely supported Democrats. Young women swung right as well, though not in such striking numbers.

Now Democrats hold a slim, 1-percentage-point advantage with young men, a group that is politically up for grabs. Around 10% of young men remain undecided. Among young women, 31% of whom supported Trump in 2024, the analysis found that support for the Republican Party had been cut to just 13%.

“Trump’s focus is not good,” said Marcos Jimenez, a 21-year-old studying to be a math teacher in Oakville, California. He voted for Trump on his economic promises, he said, only to get a war and spiraling costs.

”He’s focusing on things outside of the country like wars,” Jimenez said. “I wish he would focus more here.”

He will be supporting Democrats in the fall, he said: “They’re more for people.”

Young voters — nearly half of whom are people of color — chose Trump two years ago for many different reasons. Johnson, an immigrant from Liberia who came to Iowa at 15 and became a citizen soon after, said he had “started seeing the rise in biological males in women’s sports.”

Johnson was not alone in saying that “threw” him off. In Times/Siena polling, half of young men said they thought the Democratic Party was too far to the left.

And Johnson was passionate about the election; he said he had persuaded 15 members of his extended family to vote for Trump, too.

Now he sees bigger problems: the price of gas and housing. Seven of his friends have taken second jobs. So has he, with a day job at the plastics company and a night job at Whole Foods. The rent on his mother’s African goods store is going up, he said, and gas prices are biting.

“Trump’s becoming an old, crazy man,” he said. “He doesn’t care anymore.”

Beyond the youngest voters, the next age group — voters between the ages of 30 and 44 — has also bolted, from a 17-point advantage for Trump among men of that age to a 6-point advantage for Democrats.

“All the woke stuff happening” in the Democratic Party had pushed Remi Martinez, 44, to Trump, he said. Now Martinez, a dispatcher for a trucking company in western Kansas, regrets it.

Martinez is Hispanic and said people should not assume voters like him are opposed to deportations: “I don’t want rapists in my neighborhood either,” he said.

But, he added, Trump has swept up “hardworking people who have been here for years.”

So many people have been taken from his town of Garden City, a meatpacking area with large Hispanic population, that the town seems “shut down,” he said.

“They were just after everybody,” he said, “pulling over everybody.”

He plans to vote for Adam Hamilton, the Democrat, in the Kansas Senate race and is encouraging his daughter, who’s in her 20s, to support James Talarico in Texas, he said.

“The government needs to have checks and balances,” he said.

Although the movement among young women was smaller, Republicans did get an uptick of support in 2024. Today, Democrats’ lead with the group is vast at nearly 70 percentage points.

Bridges, 22, grew up in rural central Texas, and as a Catholic, she was put off by Democrats’ positions on transgender youth issues. Two years ago, she cast her first ballot — for Trump.

Now starting graduate school in international affairs at Texas A&M University, she does not like how Trump is treating America’s allies. She was angry when foreign aid was slashed — her faith calls for helping those in need — and when Trump barred news outlets from the White House.

She said that she found Trump’s dismissive treatment of the Epstein files appalling, and that his administration was going in reverse on women.

“I’m sure you know who Andrew Tate is,” she said, referring to the online influencer known for his chauvinistic views and who was arrested on charges of rape and sex trafficking. “This administration is pushing for that kind of man right now — hyper, hypermasculine.

“I’m a Catholic conservative, not a Christian nationalist,” she added. “We have respect for women.”

Bridges said she did not find the Democratic Party appealing either; she did not trust Talarico, in part because of his change in position on transgender athletes, and in part because she didn’t like his mixing of faith and politics. She said she did not plan to vote in this election.

That would not be unusual. In 2022 — the last midterm election — only about 30% of voters younger than 30 showed up at the ballot box, compared with close to 70% of voters older than 65.

Unlike older voters, who tend to be more set in their partisan ways at the ballot box, young voters are still trying ideas on for size.

Liam Howard, 26, grew up in a politically conservative family in New Hampshire that regularly watched Fox News and listened to Glenn Beck, the conservative talk show host. In his early voting years, he said he considered himself a libertarian and voted for Republicans in 2018, his first election.

Then he went to college and “realized that liberals aren’t actually weird,” he said.

Howard now makes emergency lights for vehicles and lives with his parents because housing in southern New Hampshire has risen out of his reach.

“I can’t even afford a crappy studio apartment working 40 hours a week in a factory,” he said. “Thirty years ago, my job would have bought a house. It’s insane.”

That economic reality has drawn him to politicians like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. About 30% of younger voters said they would prefer a democratic socialist, more so than any other age group, according to Times/Siena polling.

Howard is one of them, and as a democratic socialist, he said he did not vote for president in 2024. Kamala Harris lacked ideas, he said, and he didn’t like her position on Israel. But he is excited by the crop of democratic socialists who have won primaries around the country this season and said he felt motivated to vote.

Despite the broad turn away from the Republican Party, about 44% of young men still prefer Republicans in this fall’s elections. Conner Fredrickson, a 28-year-old who owns an information technology business and lives in Phoenix, said the president was “trying to build America back, make us stronger, make us more independent.”

He added, “Is he doing everything right? No. But nobody does everything right.”

Many younger voters said they were looking for anyone — regardless of party — who could help make life affordable. That has brought a new fluidity to the electorate.

Ryan Gellings, 25, a grocery marketer in Kansas City, Kansas, considers himself a Republican. He is Catholic, likes small government and supported Trump in 2016, though he was too young to vote for him. He still likes what he calls Republican values, but he thinks Republican politicians are mostly yes-men for Trump. To his regret, he said, he voted for Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for president in 2024.

Now he is drawn to candidates like Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez, Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York and Rep.Thomas Massie, R-Ky., because, he said, they seem deeply committed to doing something about the cost of living, no matter which way the political winds are blowing.

“I love that Mamdani is taking care of his people,” he said. “If money is going to be wasted, it may as well be for the people,” Gellings added.

One-third of voters age 18 to 29 say neither party is focused on the right things, the highest share of any age group.

Gellings said he was planning to vote for Hamilton. But mostly, he is frustrated with both parties.

“We’re confused and ready to move — anywhere at this point,” he said. “We are tired of the current conversation.”

news.title: Kansas Democrat Adam Hamilton Backed Obama Clemency Expansion Before Recipients Faced Murder, Cocaine, Fentanyl Cases
news.text:
Kansas Democrat Senate nominee Adam Hamilton served on a Barack Obama advisory council that recommended expanding eligibility for presidential commutations and pardons and considering targeted categorical grants of commutations and pardons, years before several people whose sentences Obama commuted faced new criminal cases involving murder, oxycodone pills containing fentanyl, and cocaine intended for sale.

Hamilton, the founding and senior pastor of the Church of the Resurrection who is challenging incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS), served on President Barack Obama’s Advisory Council on Faith-based and Neighborhood Partnerships.

In a 2016 report, Strengthening Efforts to Increase Opportunity and End Poverty, the council recommended that Obama “expand eligibility to receive commutations and pardons” and consider “Targeted Categorical Grants” while looking for ways to streamline the clemency process. All members of the council except Naseem Kourosh, who abstained, voted to make the recommendations to Obama and his administration.

The report specifically praised results from Obama’s Clemency Initiative, a program announced in 2014 under which certain incarcerated people could apply to be pardoned or receive a commuted sentence if they would have received a shorter sentence if convicted at the time, had served at least ten years of their total sentence, maintained good conduct throughout their prison term, and did not have a violent past record or ties to drug cartels.

“The outcomes of this program have already been favorable and we encourage the Administration to explore options to expand these efforts even further,” the council wrote.

“In view of the purposes of clemency and the unconscionable sentences that have routinely been handed out in the last few decades, we recommend that the President expand the swath of cases eligible under his program and strive to reduce the burden to file and to process these applications,” the report continued.

The council also asked Obama to consider “a Targeted Categorical Grant of commutations and pardons to specific sets of prisoners and former prisoners,” pointing to broad grants previously issued by Presidents Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter.

The report said the administration could identify categories of offenders whose sentences were, by definition, too long for their crimes and others who, after serving time, had reintegrated sufficiently to merit removal of the “cloud of conviction.”

Several people whose sentences Obama commuted later faced new criminal cases, including Alton Mills, who was accused of murder in an Illinois road-rage shooting; Joseph Burgos, who was charged after investigators said they found 1,983 oxycodone pills containing 212 grams of fentanyl; and Bobby Gill, who was sentenced to five years in federal prison after pleading guilty in a cocaine case.

Illinois State Police accused Mills of killing Linda Chatman during an Interstate 57 road-rage incident in Posen.

According to the Chicago Sun-Times, police said Mills became “angry that the victim cut him off” before firing three times into her vehicle. Chatman was struck in the head and killed.

At a detention hearing, a judge denied Mills’s request to be released while awaiting trial on a murder charge.

Burgos subsequently became a suspect in a drug-trafficking investigation.

According to the Chicago Sun-Times, the Drug Enforcement Administration wiretapped Burgos’s phone during the investigation. On April 13, 2019, his phone registered in Midland, Texas, and DEA agents saw him heading toward Chicago before stopping him at the Greyhound bus station.

Investigators said they found 1,983 oxycodone pills containing 212 grams of fentanyl.

Burgos had two previous federal drug convictions, including one in the early 1990s that resulted in a 360-month prison sentence. That sentence was commuted in 2015.

Burgos was charged in 2020 with distribution of a controlled substance and was being held at the Winnebago County Jail in Rockford at the time of the 2023 Chicago Sun-Times report.

Gill had served approximately 25 years behind bars before returning home in 2015. According to the San Antonio Express-News, Obama’s clemency initiative freed 1,715 federal inmates as part of a broader criminal justice reform effort.

Twenty-one months later, Gill was arrested again after authorities found him in possession of more than two pounds of cocaine they alleged he intended to sell.

Gill pleaded guilty to charges related to the arrest and was sentenced in 2018 to five years in federal prison, with credit for time served since February.

The council’s clemency recommendation was not Hamilton’s only involvement in an Obama-era report addressing criminal justice and immigration issues. 

The Obama faith-based advisory council also discussed immigration in a January 2016 report, stating, “The failure to provide a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants has denied countless hardworking people opportunities to earn a living, support their families, and advance their education in this country.” The report further said immigration enforcement could separate parents from children and impose economic hardships on mixed-status families.

Hamilton also said in January that if the ICE protests and enforcement actions he described in Minneapolis occurred in Kansas City, he would “want to be out there with people” protesting.

Breitbart News reported on October 14 that Hamilton voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election and contributed $500 to her campaign on July 23, 2024, two days after President Joe Biden ended his reelection bid. Hamilton said he was drawn to Harris in part by a concern for “the weak, the vulnerable” and said “justice weighs heavily for me,” while describing President Donald Trump as a “disrupter” whose decision-making concerned him. Hamilton also said the events of January 6 were a “disqualifier” for Trump from his perspective, though he added after Trump’s election that he would pray for him and “do the best I can to be supportive.”

Kansas Democrat Senate nominee Adam Hamilton served on a Barack Obama advisory council that recommended expanding eligibility for presidential commutations and pardons and considering targeted categorical grants of commutations and pardons, years before several people whose sentences Obama commuted faced new criminal cases involving murder, oxycodone pills containing fentanyl, and cocaine intended for sale.

news.title: Just A Reminder That Trump Has Repeatedly Insulted Women Who Failed The Bar
news.text:
President Donald Trump last week touted new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia as a “brilliant” accredited “attorney,” only for her to admit Thursday that she never passed the bar examination — and Trump’s rather relevant insults from the past came back to bite him.

Zacharia on Tuesday delivered a shaky debut press briefing and raised serious questions about whether she is actually a lawyer or an attorney, initially claiming to have passed the bar while living in China before admitting she never completed that fundamental requirement.

Her new boss ultimately has a lengthy history of insulting female political figures who haven’t.

“We’re killing her in the polls, because the American people don’t want her,” Trump told reporters in October 2024 about then-Vice President Kamala Harris. “She didn’t pass her bar exam. She’s not a smart person. She’s not a person that should represent our country.”

Trump even went as far as calling her a “moron” — despite Harris passing the bar exam on her second attempt in 1990.

The MAGA leader similarly dismissed former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton during his 2016 presidential campaign against her.

“She went to Washington, D.C., she took her bar exam and she failed, right?” Trump said during a rally at the time. “Oh, she’s a genius. No, no, she failed on a bar exam.” Clinton failed her D.C. bar exam in 1973, but went on to pass the Arkansas bar.

Trump appeared rather excited to announce his new press secretary was “distinguished.”

“Katie is a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University, and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney, and a frequent Commentator on outlets, including Fox News and Newsmax,” he wrote last week on his Truth Social platform, adding: “Good luck Katie!”

Zacharia told a reporter twice Tuesday that she passed the bar “when I moved to China.”

She told The New York Times on Wednesday that she couldn’t hear the question over the sound of Trump’s presidential helicopter, claiming, “I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” Zacharia ultimately admitted Thursday that she never passed the bar.

The Wall Street Journal has cited one person with direct knowledge of the matter that Zacharia sat for the California bar after graduating from Pepperdine in 2011, but didn’t pass. She worked at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing before joining the Trump administration.

At least two nonprofits are now demanding investigations into how Zacharia has represented herself, and while the scandal might privately have embarrassed Trump after his glowing praise, the MAGA leader has notably even accidentally insulted himself from time to time.
news.author: Marco Margaritoff
